Mains: inclusive growth meeting inclusiveness and sustainability together (2019); intra- and inter-generational equity in inclusive growth (2020); is inclusive growth possible under a market economy, and the significance of financial inclusion (2022); growth led by labour productivity and a job-creating growth pattern (2022).

Chapter 42Urbanisation and Demography

How the size, age and location of a population change over time, and how towns and cities, migration and the census record and shape that change.

Why it matters

Population and urban data feed most planning and policy questions. Questions test census definitions, the SRS indicators, urbanisation trends, migration models and the urban missions.

42.1 Population and the Census

The Census of India, held every ten years, is conducted by the Registrar General and Census Commissioner under the Census Act 1948. The 2011 Census counted 121.08 crore people (decadal growth 17.64%, density 382 per sq. km, sex ratio 943, literacy 74.04%). Census 2027 is India’s first digital census and the first to count caste since independence (the 16th census, and the 8th after independence). It runs in two phases: houselisting from 1 April to 30 September 2026 (each state completes a 30-day window, with self-enumeration opening 15 days earlier) and population enumeration in February 2027.

Interim demographic data come from the Sample Registration System (SRS). SRS 2023 reports a crude birth rate of 18.4, crude death rate of 6.4, total fertility rate of 1.9 (below the replacement level of 2.1; Bihar 2.8, Delhi 1.2), infant mortality rate of 25 per 1,000 live births and a sex ratio at birth of 917. NFHS (National Family Health Survey) is the other major source. The concepts of TFR, population momentum and the demographic dividend are in the chapter on poverty, inequality and human development.

Data

SRS 2023: crude birth rate 18.4; crude death rate 6.4; total fertility rate 1.9 (replacement level 2.1); infant mortality rate 25 per 1,000; sex ratio at birth 917.

42.2 Urban settlements

Category Definition (Census of India)
Statutory town Place governed by an urban local body: municipal corporation, municipality, cantonment board or notified town area committee (4,041 in 2011)
Census town Administratively rural but with population ≥ 5,000, ≥ 75% of male main workers in non-agriculture and density ≥ 400 per sq. km (3,894 in 2011, up from 1,362 in 2001)
Outgrowth Village or part of one contiguous to a town with urban features (railway colony, university campus, port); 981 in 2011
Urban agglomeration A town with adjoining outgrowths, or contiguous towns; must include at least one statutory town and have a population of at least 20,000

Towns are graded: Class I (1 lakh and above), II (50,000–99,999), III (20,000–49,999), IV (10,000–19,999), V (5,000–9,999), VI (below 5,000). A million-plus city has 10 lakh or more (53 in 2011, up from 35 in 2001); a mega city has 1 crore or more (Greater Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata).

42.3 Urbanisation trends

Metric Census 2001 Census 2011
Urban population 286.1 million 377.1 million
Level of urbanisation 27.81% 31.16%
Decadal urban growth 31.47% 31.80%
Decadal rural growth 18.09% 12.18%
Urban sex ratio 900 926

2011 was the first census when the absolute increase in urban population (91.0 million) exceeded the rural increase (90.5 million). Goa (62.17%), Mizoram, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Maharashtra were the most urbanised states; Himachal Pradesh (10.03%) and Bihar (11.29%) among the least. Delhi (97.5%) and Chandigarh lead the UTs. Maharashtra has the largest absolute urban population, followed by Uttar Pradesh.

Exam tip

Urbanisation: 27.81% (2001) to 31.16% (2011). 2011 was the first census in which the absolute increase in urban population (91.0 million) exceeded the rural increase (90.5 million).

Urban growth is driven by natural increase, reclassification of rural areas as census towns, and migration; the Indian pattern is top-heavy, with over 70% of urban people in Class I cities while small and medium towns lack funds and jobs. Census 2011 counted 65.5 million slum dwellers; a slum is notified, recognised or identified (a compact area of at least 300 people or 60–70 households in poor, congested housing without water and sanitation).

42.4 Migration

Everett Lee’s push-pull model (1966): migration depends on factors at origin (push: agricultural distress, disguised unemployment), destination (pull: wages, jobs, services), intervening obstacles (distance, cost) and personal factors. Ravenstein’s laws (1885): most migrants move short distances; step migration; every stream creates a counter-stream; women migrate more over short distances, men over long.

Harris-Todaro model (1970): a rural worker migrates if the expected urban wage exceeds the rural wage. Expected urban wage = Wu × Pe, where Pe = Eu / Lu (probability of an urban job). Creating urban jobs without raising rural productivity can draw in more migrants than jobs, raising urban unemployment (the Todaro paradox).

Exam tip

Harris-Todaro: a rural worker migrates if the expected urban wage exceeds the rural wage; expected wage = urban wage x probability of an urban job (urban employed / urban labour force).

Census 2011 recorded 455.7 million internal migrants (37.6% of the population; 314.5 million, 30.6% in 2001). Rural-to-rural migration is the largest stream, driven mostly by marriage among women; rural-to-urban migration is dominated by men moving for work. Economic Survey 2016-17, using railway travel data, estimated about 9 million inter-state movements a year, with Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal as main sources.

Data

Census 2011: 455.7 million internal migrants, 37.6% of the population (30.6% in 2001). Rural-to-rural is the largest stream, driven mostly by marriage among women.

Chapter 43Education and Health

The two social sectors that build human capital: how a country schools its people and keeps them healthy, and what the state spends and regulates to do so.

Why it matters

Schooling and health build human capital. Questions test Article 21A and the RTE Act, the NEP 2020 structure, health spending shares and Ayushman Bharat.

43.1 Education: status

Education is on the Concurrent List (since the 42nd Amendment, 1976). Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes elementary education a fundamental right, operationalised by the Right to Education Act 2009, in force from 1 April 2010.

Indicator Value
Literacy, Census 2011 74% overall; 82% male; 65% female
GER, primary (UDISE+ 2024-25) 90.9%
GER, upper primary 90.3%
GER, secondary 78.7% (NER 47.5%; dropout 11.5%)
GER, higher secondary 58.4%
GER, higher education 27% (AISHE 2019-20)
Total school enrolment, 2024-25 24.69 crore; girls 48.5%
Public expenditure on education about 3% of GDP in the notes (target 6%)

UDISE+ (Unified District Information System for Education Plus) is the Ministry of Education’s school database; AISHE (All India Survey on Higher Education) covers higher education; ASER (Annual Status of Education Report, run by Pratham) assesses learning outcomes in rural districts. The problem is quality as much as access.

Data

UDISE+ 2024-25 GER: primary 90.9%, upper primary 90.3%, secondary 78.7%, higher secondary 58.4%.

43.2 National Education Policy 2020

NEP 2020 replaced the National Policy on Education 1986. It was drafted by a committee under K. Kasturirangan and is aligned with SDG 4.

  • Structure 5+3+3+4: Foundational (ages 3–8: three years pre-school plus Classes 1–2), Preparatory (Classes 3–5), Middle (6–8), Secondary (9–12).
  • Foundational literacy and numeracy: NIPUN Bharat mission; Vidya Pravesh play-based module for Grade 1.
  • Mother tongue or regional language as medium at least till Grade 5, preferably Grade 8; three-language formula.
  • Vocational education from Class 6 with internships; PARAKH as the national assessment centre; four-year integrated B.Ed.
  • Higher education: Higher Education Commission of India as single regulator (excluding medical and legal), Academic Bank of Credit, multiple entry and exit, National Research Foundation, National Educational Technology Forum.
  • Targets: universal education from ECCE to secondary by 2030; 100% GER in pre-school to secondary by 2030; 50% GER in higher education by 2035; public spending of 6% of GDP.
Exam tip

NEP 2020 (Kasturirangan committee) replaced the 1986 policy: 5+3+3+4 structure, foundational literacy and numeracy through NIPUN Bharat, mother tongue as medium at least till Grade 5; the funding goal is 6% of GDP.

Criticisms: centralisation against state autonomy; privatisation and commercialisation; vague implementation roadmap; limited consultation; overlap with the RTE Act; the digital divide; a funding gap against the 6% goal.

43.3 Health: status

Health is a State subject; the Centre funds centrally sponsored schemes (the National Health Mission, merging the rural and urban missions). The National Health Accounts (NHA) for 2022-23 (released May 2026) show:

Data

National Health Accounts 2022-23: government health expenditure 1.43% of GDP (1.15% in 2013-14); per capita Rs 2,786; government share of total health expenditure 43.7% (28.6% in 2013-14).

  • Government health expenditure 1.43% of GDP (1.15% in 2013-14; 1.48% on the new GDP series).
  • Per capita government health expenditure Rs 2,786 (Rs 1,042 in 2013-14).
  • Government share of total health expenditure 43.7% (28.6% in 2013-14); out-of-pocket spending is falling, and was about 40% in earlier data.
  • Government health spending is 4.89% of total general government expenditure.

Older figures (2.1% of GDP total public health, doctor availability 0.7 per 1,000 against the WHO’s 1 per 1,000, institutional delivery 86% in NFHS-5, stunting 35.5%, wasting 19.3%, underweight 32.1%) come from different years. SRS 2023 shows IMR 25 and TFR 1.9 (see the chapter on urbanisation and demography).

43.4 National Health Policy 2017

  • Goal: universal access to quality healthcare without financial hardship; public health spending to rise gradually to 2.5% of GDP (by 2025); two-thirds of resources to primary care; free drugs, diagnostics and emergency care in public facilities; 2 hospital beds per 1,000.
  • Targets: life expectancy from 67.5 to 70 years (2025); TFR 2.1 (2025); IMR 28 (2019); under-five mortality 23 (2025); reduce premature NCD mortality by 25% (2025); elimination of kala-azar, filariasis (2017) and leprosy (2018).
  • Criticisms: health not made a justiciable right; the proposed health cess dropped; no clarity on State versus Concurrent List; a small share of doctors in the public sector.
Exam tip

National Health Policy 2017: public health spending to rise to 2.5% of GDP by 2025; two-thirds of resources to primary care; 2 hospital beds per 1,000.

43.5 Ayushman Bharat

Launched on the National Health Policy 2017, it shifts from a segmented to a need-based system with two arms. Funding is 60:40 between the Centre and states with legislatures, 90:10 for the north-eastern and Himalayan states, and 100% central for UTs without a legislature.

Exam tip

Ayushman Bharat funding: 60:40 Centre and states with legislatures; 90:10 for north-eastern and Himalayan states; 100% central for UTs without a legislature.

  1. Health and Wellness Centres (now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs): upgraded sub-centres and primary health centres for preventive and primary care.
  2. PM-JAY (launched 23 September 2018 at Ranchi): cashless cover up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, with pre- and post-hospitalisation care. It was designed for about 10.74 crore poor families (about 50 crore people, the bottom 40%), selected by SECC 2011 deprivation and occupational criteria. In September 2024 it was extended to all citizens aged 70 and above regardless of income (Ayushman Vay Vandana). At eight years: more than 48.5 crore Ayushman cards, about 13.25 crore hospital admissions, about Rs 2.03 lakh crore of treatment funded (to 31 August 2026), more than 38,000 empanelled hospitals, and 1.36 crore Vay Vandana cards.

The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (September 2021; National Health Authority) provides a voluntary Unique Health ID (ABHA), a Healthcare Professionals Registry, a Healthcare Facilities Registry and a sandbox for health-tech firms. Concerns: data protection (see the chapter on services and digital for the DPDP Act), digital exclusion and system failures.

43.6 Recap

  • RTE Act 2009 (Art. 21A); NEP 2020 under Kasturirangan; 5+3+3+4; 6% of GDP; 50% higher-education GER by 2035.
  • UDISE+ 2024-25 GER: 90.9 / 90.3 / 78.7 / 58.4.
  • Government health spending: 1.15% → 1.43% of GDP; NHP 2017 target 2.5%.
  • PM-JAY: Rs 5 lakh; 70+ from Sept 2024; 48.5 crore cards.
  • Funding ratio of Ayushman Bharat: 60:40, 90:10, 100%.

No previous-year questions on education and health are included here.

Chapter 44Social Structure

The pattern of religion, language, caste and tribe that makes up Indian society, and the constitutional design through which a diverse population is held together and disadvantage is corrected.

Why it matters

India’s social structure shapes its constitutional provisions and welfare design. Questions test secularism, the Eighth Schedule, classical languages, the reservation structure and recent gender and tribal programmes.

44.1 Diversity and multiculturalism

Multiculturalism has two senses: descriptive (the fact of cultural, linguistic, ethnic and religious diversity) and normative (policies and principles that secure equal treatment and recognition of diverse groups).

Thinker Idea
Will Kymlicka (Multicultural Citizenship, 1995) Liberal multiculturalism: individual autonomy needs a secure cultural context. Three group-differentiated rights: self-government (for national minorities), polyethnic (exemptions for immigrant groups, e.g. religious dress) and special representation. Permits external protections but not internal restrictions on a group’s own members
Bhikhu Parekh (Rethinking Multiculturalism) Pluralist and dialogical: rejects liberal monism; culture shapes identity; intercultural dialogue on mutual respect
Charles Taylor (The Politics of Recognition, 1992) Misrecognition harms identity; the “politics of difference” protects authenticity against assimilation

Two integration models: the melting pot (assimilation; the early United States) and the salad bowl or mosaic (cultural pluralism; Canada’s Multiculturalism Act 1988, the United Kingdom, India). The mosaic risks fragmentation; the melting pot enforces the majority’s culture.

Exam tip

Kymlicka’s three group-differentiated rights: self-government, polyethnic and special representation. Models: melting pot (assimilation) and salad bowl or mosaic (pluralism; India).

44.2 Indian secularism

India follows principled distance (Rajeev Bhargava): the state neither separates from religion as in strict American separation or French laïcité, nor identifies with one religion. It intervenes when practices violate dignity or rights (abolition of untouchability, temple entry, the 2019 ban on instant triple talaq) while protecting minority cultural institutions. The ethos is sarva dharma sambhava (equal respect to all faiths) rather than dharma nirpekshta (indifference).

Exam tip

Indian secularism is principled distance (Rajeev Bhargava): the state neither separates from religion nor identifies with one. Religious freedom: Articles 25 to 30.

Article Guarantee
14 Equality before law
15(1) No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
25 Freedom of conscience; profess, practise, propagate religion (subject to public order, morality, health)
26 Religious denominations manage their own affairs
27 No compulsory taxes for promoting a religion
28 No compulsory religious instruction in wholly State-funded schools
29 Minorities conserve language, script, culture
30 Minorities establish and administer educational institutions of their choice
Fifth and Sixth Schedules Tribal areas; autonomous district councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram (Sixth)

44.5.1 Women in the economy

  • Global Gender Gap Report 2025 (World Economic Forum): India ranked 131 of 148 countries with a score of 64.1%; the education sub-index was 97.1% and the economic participation sub-index 40.7%; women held 13.8% of seats in Parliament.
  • Female labour force participation rate: 33.9% in 2022, rising to about 40% in 2025 on a secondary-source estimate, driven largely by rural self-employment.
  • Unpaid work: women spend 299 minutes a day on unpaid domestic work against 97 minutes for men (Time Use Survey).
  • Laws and schemes: Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 (26 weeks of leave; creche for establishments with 50 or more employees); Code on Wages (equal pay for equal work); Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (reservation of one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies); Mission Shakti; National Creche Scheme; Stand-Up India (bank loans to women and SC/ST entrepreneurs).

Global Gender Gap Report 2025: India 131 of 148, score 64.1%; education sub-index 97.1%, economic participation 40.7%; women hold 13.8% of seats in Parliament.

Chapter 45Environment and Sustainable Development

How economic growth is reconciled with limits set by the environment: sustainable development, climate change and the international and Indian response to it.

Why it matters

Climate and environment questions mix treaties, India’s targets and the legal framework, and dates and numbers matter. This chapter holds them in one place.

45.1 Sustainable development

The term was first used in 1980 by the IUCN and entered mainstream policy through Our Common Future (1987), the Brundtland Report of the World Commission on Environment and Development: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own. The 2015 Sustainable Development Goals (17 goals, target year 2030) carry the idea forward; they are listed in the chapter on poverty, inequality and human development. Climate change threatens most of them: economic output (Pakistan floods 2022), food security (the 2022 South Asian heatwave and wheat export curbs), water (Aral Sea), health (European heatwave 2022), ecosystems (coral bleaching, Amazon) and migration (Bangladesh).

Exam tip

Sustainable development: first used in 1980 by the IUCN; Brundtland Report (Our Common Future) 1987; Sustainable Development Goals 2015.

45.2 Greenhouse gases and warming

Definition

The greenhouse effect is the trapping of outgoing heat by atmospheric gases; global warming is its human-driven strengthening. Main gases: carbon dioxide (fossil fuel burning, deforestation), methane (rice fields, livestock, wetlands, landfill), nitrous oxide (fertiliser, fossil fuels) and fluorinated gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF6; refrigeration, semiconductors). Black carbon is a short-lived climate pollutant. By contribution to warming: CO2 about 60%, methane 20%, N2O 6%, fluorinated gases 14%. Global warming potential is highest for SF6 and NF3.

By sector the notes give electricity and heat 25%, agriculture and forestry 24%, industry 21%, transport 14%; by country China 28%, the United States 16%, the EU 10%, India 4% (an old, rounded split; India’s per capita emissions are well below the world average).

IPCC (WMO and UNEP, 1988; Geneva) assesses scientific evidence but does not do research; its Sixth Assessment found warming of about 1.1°C since 1850; the seventh cycle began in 2023.

Exam tip

IPCC (1988): assesses scientific evidence and does not do research; its Sixth Assessment found warming of about 1.1°C since 1850.

45.3 International climate regime

Instrument Key points
Rio “sisters” (1992) UNFCCC (climate), CBD (biodiversity), UNCCD (desertification)
UNFCCC (entered into force 1994) Parent treaty; COP meets annually; principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR)
Kyoto Protocol (COP-3, 1997) Binding targets for Annex I countries; phases 2008–12 and 2013–20; market mechanisms: emissions trading, Clean Development Mechanism (the only one open to developing countries) and Joint Implementation
Bali (COP-13, 2007), Cancun (COP-16, 2010) Bali Action Plan; Green Climate Fund, Adaptation Fund
Warsaw (COP-19, 2013) Warsaw Framework for REDD+; the US$100 billion a year by 2020 goal (set earlier, at Copenhagen 2009 and Cancun 2010)
Paris Agreement (COP-21, 2015) Replaced Kyoto; keep warming well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; voluntary Nationally Determined Contributions every five years; Article 6 on carbon markets
COP-28 Dubai (2023) Loss and Damage fund operationalised
COP-29 Baku (2024) New finance goal of US$300 billion a year by 2035; Article 6 carbon-market rules

Financing bodies: the Global Environment Facility (1991), Green Climate Fund (2010; the largest), Least Developed Countries Fund and Special Climate Change Fund. The International Solar Alliance (2015; initiative of India and France, headquartered in Gurugram) follows “One Sun, One World, One Grid”.

Exam tip

Global Environment Facility 1991; Green Climate Fund 2010 (the largest); International Solar Alliance 2015 (India and France, Gurugram). Rio 1992: UNFCCC, CBD, UNCCD. Kyoto Protocol: COP-3, 1997.

Carbon pricing tools: a carbon credit is a permit to emit one tonne of CO2e; carbon trading is its sale; cap and trade sets a falling ceiling and lets low emitters sell credits; a carbon tax charges per tonne emitted (the notes cite a Rs 400 per tonne tax on coal, the old Clean Energy Cess rate). Carbon capture, green and blue carbon, and geo-engineering are further options.

45.4 India’s response

  • National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) with eight missions: Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change.
  • Panchamrit (COP-26 Glasgow, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030; cut projected emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030; reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030; net zero by 2070.
  • Updated NDC (2022): 45% intensity cut (vs 2005) and 50% non-fossil electric capacity by 2030, against the 2015 INDC of 33–35% and 40%.
  • NDC 3.0 (2031–35), approved by the Cabinet in 2026: 47% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP by 2035 (vs 2005), 60% of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources by 2035, and an additional carbon sink of 3.5–4.0 billion tonnes CO2e. India reached a 36% intensity cut by 2020, 52.57% non-fossil share in February 2026 and an additional sink of 2.29 billion tonnes by 2025.
Exam tip

NAPCC (2008): eight missions, including Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water and Green India. Panchamrit (COP-26 Glasgow, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.

India’s non-fossil capacity crossed 300 GW on 31 July 2026 (over 54% of about 552 GW installed, over 60% of the 500 GW goal): solar 164.6 GW, wind 58.1, hydro 57.2, bio-power 11.8, nuclear 8.8.

Other measures: National Green Hydrogen Mission (5 million tonnes a year by 2030), the biofuel policy (20% ethanol blending), electric-vehicle schemes (FAME, now PM E-DRIVE), energy conservation building code (Bureau of Energy Efficiency), Green Term Ahead Market, the Green Credit Programme and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022. Energy supply and power are covered in the chapter on infrastructure.

45.5 Pollution, forests and biodiversity: law and institutions

Constitutional basis. Article 48A (Directive Principle: the State shall protect and improve the environment), Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty of every citizen) and Article 21 (the Supreme Court reads the right to life to include a clean environment).

Exam tip

Article 48A: Directive Principle on the environment. Article 51A(g): Fundamental Duty. Article 21: right to life read to include a clean environment.

45.6 Recap

  • Brundtland 1987; SDGs 2030.
  • CBDR: Kyoto (binding, CDM) → Paris (voluntary NDCs, 1.5°C, Article 6).
  • COP-29: US$300 billion by 2035.

Chapter 46Farming Systems and the Food Economy

How farms are watered, cropped and organised, and how food moves from field to consumer through processing, storage, regulation and trade.

Why it matters

This chapter covers how farms are watered, cropped and organised, and how food is processed and regulated. Questions test irrigation sources, PMKSY, GM crops, organic certification and food laws.

46.1 Irrigation

Irrigation is the artificial application of water to land, a substitute or supplement for rain and basic infrastructure for production. Sources: tube wells (about 46% of irrigated area; the deep-water-table Indo-Gangetic plain and deltas), canals (24%; first in the 1950s–60s, then overtaken by wells in the 1970s; concentrated in Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Punjab), wells (17%) and tanks (12%; the peninsula, especially Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu). The percentages are on an older statistical basis.

The Indira Gandhi Canal (649 km, from Harike barrage to the Thar in Rajasthan) is the longest canal in India.

Data

Irrigation sources: tube wells about 46% of irrigated area, canals 24%. The Indira Gandhi Canal (649 km, Harike barrage to the Thar in Rajasthan) is the longest canal in India.

Method Features and use
Surface / flood: basin, furrow, border strip Basin for paddy and wheat; furrow for cotton, sugarcane, vegetables
Drip / micro 2–20 litres an hour at the root; row crops, orchards, vines; high capital cost; Meghalaya’s 200-year-old bamboo drip system
Sprinkler Uneven land and sandy soils; less water wasted

PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY), launched 1 July 2015: Har Khet Ko Pani (extend irrigation), Per Drop More Crop (micro-irrigation), watershed development and AIBP. About 24.6 million hectares of irrigation potential created or restored since 2016-17 and 110.9 lakh hectares brought under micro-irrigation (about 8% of net sown area); the 2021–26 outlay was Rs 93,068.56 crore and the 2026-27 Budget allocated Rs 6,587 crore. Per Drop More Crop has formed part of PM-RKVY since 2022-23.

Exam tip

PMKSY (1 July 2015): Har Khet Ko Pani, Per Drop More Crop, watershed development and AIBP. 110.9 lakh hectares brought under micro-irrigation.

46.2 Farming systems and cropping patterns

  • Primitive subsistence (shifting cultivation: hoe, dao, digging stick), intensive subsistence (high population pressure, labour-intensive) and commercial farming (HYV seeds, chemicals); plantations (tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane) are capital-intensive commercial farming with an industrial link.
  • Seasons: kharif, rabi and zaid.
  • Patterns: monocropping; multiple cropping: intercropping (rows, e.g. pigeon pea with sorghum), mixed cropping (no fixed pattern, e.g. wheat with mustard), sequential cropping (rice-wheat), relay cropping (the next crop sown before the first is harvested); crop rotation; ratooning (regrowth from stubble); mixed farming (crops plus livestock, fisheries, bee-keeping).
  • A sustainable food system delivers food security and nutrition for all without compromising future generations, economically, socially and environmentally (SDG 2).

46.3 Animal husbandry, dairy and fisheries

Livestock gives income, employment in the lean season, protein, a social-security asset, draught power and dung, and is more equitably distributed than land; it is largely women-led. Challenges: weak veterinary and extension services, poor market links, no insurance or credit, and degraded pasture.

  • Milk output 2024-25: 247.87 million tonnes (+3.58%), per capita availability 485 g a day; eggs 149.11 billion; meat 10.50 million tonnes (Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics 2025). India is the largest milk producer.
  • National Livestock Mission (2014-15) has four sub-missions: fodder and feed, livestock development, pig development in the North-East, skill development and extension. A separate Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying exists. The 20th Livestock Census (2019) counted about 54 crore animals, with Uttar Pradesh highest.
  • PM Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY): the Blue Revolution umbrella (central sector and centrally sponsored components) for marine, inland fisheries and aquaculture, harbours, cold chains, and “Sagar Mitra” extension workers. Fisheries are about 1.24% of GDP and 7.28% of agricultural GVA.
  • Horticulture: Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH), centrally sponsored (60:40; 90:10 for the North-East and Himalayan states); National Bamboo Mission (67% of India’s bamboo is in the North-East).
Data

2024-25: milk 247.87 million tonnes (+3.58%), per capita 485 g a day; eggs 149.11 billion; meat 10.50 million tonnes. India is the largest milk producer.

46.4 Biotechnology and seeds

  • GM crops are regulated by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. Bt cotton (since 2002) is the only commercially cultivated GM crop; Bt brinjal has been under a moratorium since 2010. The GEAC cleared GM mustard (DMH-11) for environmental release in October 2022 (about 30% yield claim) but it is contested. The government price-controlled Bt cotton seed (2016) under the Essential Commodities Act.
  • Genome-edited rice: two varieties, DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1, developed with SDN-1 editing (no foreign DNA), were announced in May 2025 with yield claims up to 30%.
  • Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act 2001: breeders get exclusive rights; farmers may save, sow, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, but not branded packaged seed; a National Gene Fund receives royalties and pays benefit-sharing and rewards for conservation.

46.5 Alternative farming systems

System Core idea
Organic farming No synthetic chemicals; manures, rotation, biocontrol. Certified under NPOP (third-party, Commerce Ministry, APEDA; export and domestic) or PGS-India (peer-based, Agriculture Ministry; domestic only); FSSAI “Jaivik Bharat” logo. Sikkim: first fully organic State (2016)
Zero Budget Natural Farming No purchased inputs: Bijamrit, Jivamrit, mulching, Waaphasa; no external fertiliser even organic, no tillage; contrasts with organic farming
Integrated Farming System Crops with livestock, fish, etc.; waste of one enterprise feeds another; ICAR has 60 models; suited to small farms
Agroecology Ecological and social principles; bottom-up, local knowledge
Conservation agriculture Minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, crop diversification
Protected cultivation Polyhouses, shade nets, plastic mulch for horticulture; high capital cost
Permaculture / smart & precision farming Design philosophy; AI, IoT, drones; small holdings (over half below 1 ha) limit uptake

Challenges to organic farming: weak supply chains, no yield-loss subsidy during conversion, scarce inputs, and brand authenticity.

Exam tip

NPOP is third-party certification (Commerce Ministry, APEDA; export and domestic); PGS-India is peer-based (Agriculture Ministry; domestic only). Sikkim: first fully organic State (2016).

46.6 Supply chain and food processing

A supply chain moves goods from supplier to customer; upstream is raw-material extraction, downstream is processing and sale. Backward and forward integration are vertical; acquiring a rival is horizontal.

The food processing industry employs about 74% of its workers in the unorganised segment (about 25 lakh units) but the organised segment adds 72% of value; 100% FDI is allowed under the automatic route, and loans to food processing and cold chains count as priority sector lending. Constraints: perishability, weak cold chain (about 25% farm-level wastage cited), low technology, skills, fragmented retail, APMC rules and multiple clearances.

Data

Food processing: about 74% of workers are in the unorganised segment, but the organised segment adds 72% of value; 100% FDI is allowed under the automatic route.

Schemes: SAMPADA (umbrella; Mega Food Parks, cold chain, agro-processing clusters; Rs 6,000 crore), PM Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME) (2020-21 to 2024-25, Rs 10,000 crore, 60:40, 35% credit-linked subsidy up to Rs 10 lakh, One District One Product), Operation Greens (tomato, onion, potato; Budget 2018-19; Rs 500 crore) and Kisan Rail (50% transport subsidy). The Price Stabilisation Fund (2014-15) finances buffer stocks of onion, potato and pulses through NAFED and SFAC.

Exam tip

SAMPADA: Rs 6,000 crore umbrella scheme. PMFME (2020-21 to 2024-25): Rs 10,000 crore, 60:40, One District One Product. Operation Greens (Budget 2018-19): tomato, onion, potato.

46.6.1 Regulation

  • Essential Commodities Act 1955 lets the Centre regulate production, supply and prices of listed items and impose stock limits; critics say it deters storage investment.
  • Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act 2007: the WDRA registers warehouses and regulates negotiable warehouse receipts; electronic NWRs (2017) enable pledge finance and trading on e-NAM (from April 2020).
  • Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 and eight older orders; FSSAI (under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, not the Director General of Health Services) sets standards, lab certification and rapid alerts; State Commissioners of Food Safety enforce.
Exam tip

Essential Commodities Act 1955 regulates supply and prices and imposes stock limits. Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act 2007: the WDRA registers warehouses and regulates negotiable warehouse receipts; electronic NWRs from 2017. The FSS Act 2006 replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954.

46.7 Recap

  • Irrigation sources: tube wells > canals > wells > tanks; PMKSY (2015).
  • Cropping: intercrop (rows) vs mixed (no pattern) vs sequential vs relay.
  • GEAC regulates GM; Bt cotton only commercial crop; PPVFR Act 2001.
  • NPOP (third party, export) vs PGS-India (peer, domestic).
  • ZBNF adds no external inputs; organic adds manures.
  • FSS Act 2006 replaced PFA 1954; WDRA and NWRs; ECA 1955.

(ii) The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is under the charge of Director General of Health Services in the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Which is/are correct? [UPSC 2018]

  • (b) (ii) only

Q2. With reference to organic farming in India: (i) NPOP is operated under the guidelines of the Union Ministry of Rural Development. (ii) APEDA functions as the Secretariat for the implementation of NPOP. (iii) Sikkim has become India’s first fully organic State. Which is/are correct? [UPSC 2018]

  • (a) (i) & (ii) only
  • (b) (ii) & (iii) only

Mains: crops and cropping patterns, millets (2018); Sikkim organic State (2018); National Horticulture Mission (2018); Integrated Farming System (2019, 2022); the rice-wheat system (2020); crop diversification (2021); micro-irrigation and the water crisis (2021); supermarkets in the supply chain (2018); food processing policy, challenges and scope (2019, 2020, 2022); upstream and downstream bottlenecks in marketing of agricultural products (2022).

Chapter 47Infrastructure

The roads, rails, ports, airports, power and logistics on which every other sector depends, and the ways in which the state and private capital finance and run them.

Why it matters

Infrastructure sets the cost of doing everything else. Questions test PPP models, the Hybrid Annuity Model, corridors and ports, the logistics policy and coal and power reforms.

47.1 Why infrastructure matters

Infrastructure (roads, railways, ports, airports, power, telecom, water, logistics) is basic capital for growth. After independence the state built it; after 1991 it sought private capital to fill the gap, but the capital-intensive, long-gestation nature of projects keeps the public sector central. Public capital expenditure rose from about Rs 2 lakh crore (2014-15) to Rs 12.2 lakh crore in the 2026-27 Union Budget (Rs 11.2 lakh crore in 2025-26 BE).

47.2 Models of delivery

  • EPC (Engineering, Procurement, Construction): the government pays a contractor to build; the owner operates. Not a PPP.
  • Cost-plus: the buyer reimburses cost and adds a fixed margin; used when cost is uncertain; encourages inflated costs.
  • PPP (Public-Private Partnership): a private partner builds and operates or maintains for the project life under a concession agreement selected by competitive bidding, usually through a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV). The risk-allocation principle: each risk to the party best able to bear it (government: clearances, land, political risk; private: design, construction, maintenance). The Department of Economic Affairs defines a PPP as a contract for an infrastructure service on payment of user charges. Stages: identification, development, procurement, contract management.
  • BOT (build-operate-transfer), BOOT (build-own-operate-transfer; ownership gives collateral), DBFOT (design-build-finance-operate-transfer).
  • Viability Gap Funding (VGF): a one-time upfront grant to make an economically viable but financially unviable PPP bankable.
  • Problems: aggressive bids to win revenue share, traffic risk loaded on the private party, land and clearance burdens shifted to it, no renegotiation framework, and a large share of stressed bank assets. India’s telecom is the PPP success story.

47.3 Roads

Model Description
EPC Lowest-cost contractor builds, government maintains (not PPP)
BOT-Toll Private party builds and tolls; picks bid for maximum revenue share or minimum VGF; bears traffic risk
BOT-Annuity Private party gets fixed annual payment; no traffic risk
Hybrid Annuity Model (2016) 40% of cost paid during construction by progress, 60% as annuities after completion; the private partner bears construction and maintenance risk but only part of financing risk
TOT (Toll-Operate-Transfer) NHAI leases built highways (about 30 years) for an upfront payment, recycling funds into new roads

The National Highways Development Programme (1998; 55,792 km planned) was folded into Bharatmala Pariyojana (economic corridors, inter-corridor and feeder routes, border and coastal roads, expressways). The national highway network has grown from 91,287 km (2014) to about 1,46,572 km (March 2026) with 45,516 km at four lanes or more; 22,590 km of Bharatmala roads were complete by March 2026. Roads carry about 69% of freight and 90% of passengers.

Data

National highways grew from 91,287 km (2014) to about 1,46,572 km (March 2026). NHDP (1998) was folded into Bharatmala Pariyojana.

47.4 Railways

Indian Railways links markets and carries bulk goods for energy, steel and agriculture; a multiplier above 5 is estimated of railway investment on output (backward linkage 3.3, forward linkage 2.5) and calls rail six times more energy-efficient than roads. 100% FDI is allowed in rail infrastructure (automatic route) but not in train operations and safety. Reforms: the Bibek Debroy Committee (separation of infrastructure and train operations; independent regulator) and the Rail Development Authority (approved 2017). Station redevelopment models: PPP, collaboration with foreign governments and the Swiss Challenge; the 2022 decision moved the Mumbai, New Delhi and Ahmedabad stations to EPC.

Dedicated Freight Corridors (DFCCIL, a 100% Railways SPV): Eastern (Ludhiana–Sonnagar–Kolkata, 1,835 km) and Western (Delhi–Rewari–Vadodara–Mumbai, 1,483 km), with 100 km/h freight speed against an average of 26 km/h now. The 2026-27 Budget announced new DFCs and seven high-speed rail corridors (Mumbai–Pune, Pune–Hyderabad, Hyderabad–Bengaluru, Hyderabad–Chennai, Chennai–Bengaluru, Delhi–Varanasi, Varanasi–Siliguri). Electrification of the network stands at 99.6% (July 2026). Railway capital outlay rose from Rs 32,000 crore (2014) to Rs 2.78 lakh crore (2026-27). Mumbai–Ahmedabad is the first bullet-train corridor.

Exam tip

Dedicated Freight Corridors: Eastern (Ludhiana-Sonnagar-Kolkata, 1,835 km) and Western (Delhi-Rewari-Vadodara-Mumbai, 1,483 km); freight speed 100 km/h against an average of 26 km/h.

Industrial corridors: Delhi–Mumbai (DMIC), Bangalore–Mumbai, Chennai–Bangalore, Visakhapatnam–Chennai and Amritsar–Kolkata; a National Industrial Corridor Development Authority integrates them. SEZs are covered in the chapter on trade policy.

47.5 Ports, shipping and waterways

India has 13 major ports (central) and about 187 minor ports, and a 7,500 km coastline. Sagarmala (500+ projects under four pillars: port modernisation, connectivity, port-led industrialisation including 14 Coastal Economic Zones, and coastal community development) aims to cut logistics cost. Relative transport cost by road : rail : water = 18 : 6 : 1. The first port PPP was a JNPT terminal (BOT, 30 years). The Major Port Authorities Act 2021 replaced the 1963 Major Port Trusts Act, set a board for each major port and allowed tariff-setting by concessionaires. Major port capacity rose from 873 to 1,728 million tonnes a year (2014 to 2026); 111 national waterways are designated, 32 operational.

Exam tip

13 major ports, about 187 minor ports, 7,500 km coastline. Sagarmala: 500+ projects, four pillars, 14 Coastal Economic Zones.

47.6 Airports and aviation

The Airports Authority of India (1995) manages airports; AERA (2009) regulates tariffs at major airports (over 35 lakh passengers a year). Airport PPPs began in 2005-06 with Delhi (GMR) and Mumbai (GVK) on a revenue-share model (Delhi shared 45.99% with the government); Bangalore and Hyderabad followed, and six AAI airports were leased in 2019 on a highest per-passenger-fee basis. The UDAN / Regional Connectivity Scheme (April 2017) caps fares (Rs 2,500 for about one hour or 500 km) and pays airlines VGF from a regional connectivity fund (Centre:state 80:20), with competitive bidding on minimum VGF. Operational airports have risen from 74 (2014) to 165 (July 2026).

47.7 Logistics

Logistics cost is estimated at about 13% of GDP (against about 8% in developed economies); the National Logistics Policy 2022 targets single-digit cost and a top-25 rank in the Logistics Performance Index by 2030 through a Comprehensive Logistics Action Plan (eight areas) and the Unified Logistics Interface Platform. Multimodal Logistics Parks (35 planned; Jogighopa in Assam first) allow hub-and-spoke freight with aggregation, warehousing and customs.

Exam tip

Logistics cost: 13% of GDP against about 8% in developed economies. National Logistics Policy 2022 targets single-digit cost and a top-25 Logistics Performance Index rank by 2030.

47.8 Energy and power

  • Coal: nationalised in 1973 (Coal India monopoly); captive-block allocation without bidding led to the “Coalgate” scandal and the Supreme Court cancelled allocations in 2014. The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act 2015 allows e-auction of blocks, commercial mining and sale of coal, with proceeds going to the states. The MMDR Act 1957 (amended) grants 50-year leases through auctions, adds auction premium, and sets up District Mineral Foundations. Mineral rights belong to states, except for coal, petroleum and atomic minerals which are regulated by the Centre.
  • Power: governed by the Electricity Act 2003 (delicensing of generation, open access subject to a cross-subsidy surcharge, power exchanges since 2008). Distribution is the weak link: state DISCOMs with AT&C losses of about 20–22%, cross-subsidy and populist tariffs; UDAY did not fix structure. The Electricity Amendment Bill 2021 proposed delicensing distribution and DBT of subsidies. Generation capacity (31 January 2023): coal 51%, gas 6%, nuclear 1.7%, renewables 41%, total 411 GW; by 31 July 2026 total installed capacity was about 552 GW with over 300 GW non-fossil (see the chapter on environment and sustainable development). Renewable Purchase Obligations and Renewable Energy Certificates (1 MWh each) support clean power.
  • Oil and gas: NELP (profit sharing, 1997-98 onward) was replaced in 2016 by HELP (single licence, Open Acreage Licensing Policy, revenue sharing, marketing and pricing freedom, reduced royalty of 7.5%, 5% and 2% for shallow, deep and ultra-deep water). The Kirit Parikh Committee recommended pricing of legacy (APM) gas linked to crude with a floor of US$4 and ceiling of US$6.5 per MMBtu. A 15% share of gas in the energy mix by 2030 is the stated goal.
  • Real estate: RERA 2016 requires registration of projects above 500 sq. m or 8 units, 70% of receipts in a separate account, disclosure, and penalties including up to 3 years’ imprisonment.
Exam tip

UPSC Civil Services Examination 2019: coal was nationalised under Indira Gandhi (1973); blocks are now allotted by e-auction under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act 2015, not by lottery. Coalgate allocations were cancelled in 2014.

47.9 Urban infrastructure and finance

Urban missions (Smart Cities, AMRUT, PMAY-U) are in the chapter on urbanisation and demography. Smart Cities used an SPV per city with 50:50 State/ULB equity and area-based development (retrofit, redevelopment, greenfield); AMRUT adopted a project approach for water, sewerage, drainage, transport and green space. Value Capture Finance taps land value gains created by public investment: additional Floor Area Ratio premiums, land pooling, transferable development rights, change-of-land-use fees.

Financing vehicles: InvITs and REITs are SEBI-regulated trusts that pool money to invest in infrastructure and real estate (at least 80% in revenue-generating assets). The National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF, 2015) is a quasi-sovereign wealth fund with a 49% government stake. The 2026-27 Budget added an Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund for lenders.

Exam tip

InvITs and REITs: SEBI-regulated trusts with at least 80% in revenue-generating assets. NIIF (2015): quasi-sovereign wealth fund with a 49% government stake.

47.10 Pipelines and master plans

  • National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP, 2020-25): projected investment of Rs 102 lakh crore; energy 24%, roads 19%, urban 16%, railways 13%; funding Centre 39%, states 39%, private sector 22%.
  • National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP 1.0, launched 23 August 2021): Rs 6 lakh crore of brownfield asset leasing over FY22–FY25 (through PPP concessions and InvITs, not privatisation), about 90% achieved. NMP 2.0 (launched 24 February 2026): “Asset Monetisation Plan 2025–30” with potential of Rs 16.72 lakh crore including Rs 5.8 lakh crore of private investment; sectors include roads, railways, power, oil and gas, civil aviation, ports, telecom, coal and mines; monitored by a Core Group of Secretaries on Asset Monetisation. Press reports of “Rs 10 lakh crore” appear for the same plan.
  • PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan (October 2021): a digital GIS platform with about 200 data layers that brings ministries together to plan multimodal connectivity; the Network Planning Group evaluates projects (396 projects worth about Rs 18.66 lakh crore by August 2026).
Data

NIP 2020-25: Rs 102 lakh crore; energy 24%, roads 19%, urban 16%, railways 13%; funding Centre 39%, States 39%, private 22%. NMP 1.0 launched 23 August 2021.

47.11 Recap

  • EPC ≠ PPP; BOT-Toll / Annuity / Hybrid Annuity (40:60) / TOT.
  • VGF = upfront grant to make PPPs viable; SPV = project company.
  • DFC Eastern 1,835 km, Western 1,483 km; Sagarmala; UDAN fare cap Rs 2,500.
  • Coal: Coalgate → 2015 Act (auctions); MMDR: 50-year leases, DMF.
  • HELP/OALP revenue sharing; Parikh gas price band $4–6.5.
  • InvIT/REIT 80% rule; NIIF 49% government.
  • NIP Rs 102 lakh crore; NMP 1.0 Rs 6 lakh crore; NMP 2.0 Rs 16.72 lakh crore.
  • Public capex FY27 Rs 12.2 lakh crore.

47.12 Revision

Q1. Consider the following statements: [UPSC 2019]

  1. Coal sector was nationalised by the Government of India under Indira Gandhi.
  2. Now, coal blocks are allocated on lottery basis.
  3. Till recently, India imported coal to meet the shortage of domestic supply, but now India is self-sufficient in coal production. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

    • (a) (i) only
    • (b) (ii) & (iii) only
    • (c) (iii) only
    • (d) (i), (ii) & (iii)

Mains: investment as capital formation and the design of a concession agreement (2020); infrastructure investment and inclusive growth (2021); PPP and railway station redevelopment (2022); India meeting 50 per cent of energy needs from renewables by 2030 (2022).

RevisionRevision File

One page per chapter, 47 chapters: core idea, definitions, formulas, key numbers, comparisons and quick recall.

Revision · Chapter 1Economic Organisation and Systems

Core idea

Economics studies how societies allocate scarce resources that have alternative uses to satisfy unlimited wants (Robbins, 1932). Scarcity forces choice, and every choice has an opportunity cost. Every society must answer what, how and for whom to produce; market, command and mixed economies answer through different institutions. The circular flow shows income and spending moving between sectors, and it balances when leakages equal injections.

Definitions

  • Opportunity cost: value of the next best alternative given up (not "all alternatives").
  • Ceteris paribus: a law is stated with all other variables held constant, to isolate one cause-and-effect link.
  • Value in use vs value in exchange: total usefulness vs purchasing power in the market. Price follows marginal utility and scarcity, not total utility.
  • PPF: maximum combinations of two goods with fixed resources and technology. On the curve = efficient; inside = under-use; outside = unattainable now (needs growth).
  • MRT: slope of the PPF; how much of one good is given up for one more unit of the other.
  • Closed economy: no external sector (no exports or imports). Open economy: trades with the rest of the world.
  • Leakages: savings, taxes, imports. Injections: investment, government spending, exports.

Formulas

S + T + M = I + G + X   S savings, T taxes, M imports, I investment, G government spending, X exports. Leakages above injections: demand and output fall. Injections above leakages: demand expands; near full capacity, demand-pull inflation.

Wheat = 30 − S − S² (S = steel, lakh tonnes; the hypothetical PPF in the chapter). At S = 3: wheat = 30 − 3 − 9 = 18.

Key numbers (hypothetical examples from the chapter)

ItemValue
Wheat given up per extra lakh tonne of steel (A to E)2, 4, 6, 8: cost rises, so the PPF is concave
Leakages: S 200 + T 300 + M 150Rs 650 crore
Injections: I 250 + G 300 + X 100Rs 650 crore (balanced)
After I falls to 200 and G to 250Injections 550, Rs 100 crore below leakages: output and employment fall

Dates: Robbins definition 1932; state-led planning with licence-quota-permit raj 1947 to 1991; LPG reforms from 1991.

Comparison

MarketCommandMixed
OwnershipPrivateStateBoth
Who decidesBuyers and sellers, through pricesCentral planning authorityMarket decides most; state steers some
Fails onPublic goods, inequality, externalitiesCalculation (Mises)India
Three central questionsDecision
WhatConsumer vs capital goods; civil vs defence
HowLabour-intensive or capital-intensive technique
For whomRent (land), wages (labour), interest (capital), profit (enterprise)

Quick recall

  1. What is a closed economy?
    Show answer

    an economy with no external sector: neither exports nor imports.

  2. Why is the PPF concave?
    Show answer

    opportunity cost rises, because resources are not equally good at both jobs.

  3. If S + T + M exceeds I + G + X, what happens to demand and output?
    Show answer

    both fall.

  4. Why is water cheap and a diamond dear?
    Show answer

    price follows marginal utility and scarcity: water is abundant (marginal utility near zero), diamonds are scarce.

  5. What did the state hold in India from 1947 to 1991?
    Show answer

    the "commanding heights" (heavy industry, banking, utilities), under the licence-quota-permit raj.

Revision · Chapter 2Sectors and Goods Typology

Core idea

An economy is split by activity (primary, secondary, tertiary), ownership and formality. Whether a good is final or intermediate, consumption or capital, depends on end use, not on what it physically is. Goods are sorted again by two tests, excludable and rival, which decide whether the market can supply them.

Definitions

  • Final good: has crossed the boundary of production; value counted in GDP. Intermediate good: remains inside production; value already inside the final good.
  • Capital good: produced, durable, used again as an input, and not transformed in use. The same item can be a capital good or a consumer durable by user.
  • Depreciation: foreseen wear and obsolescence. Capital loss: unforeseen destruction (disaster, war); not deducted from net product.
  • Factors and returns: entrepreneur – profit; capital – interest; natural resources – rent; labour – wages.
  • Free-rider problem: nobody can be stopped from using a public good, so the market under-supplies it; the state finances it through taxation.
  • Tragedy of the commons (Hardin, 1968): self-interest over-uses a common pool resource. Answers: property rights, quotas, community governance (Ostrom).
  • Publicly provided ≠ public good: a public good is both non-excludable and non-rival.
  • Merit / demerit goods: differ on externalities. Veblen and Giffen goods are the two exceptions to the law of demand.

Formulas

Gross investment = GFCF + net acquisition of valuables + change in inventories
Net investment = gross investment − depreciation (imports of capital goods add to investment; exports subtract).

Sum of value added at each stage = value of the final good (bread example: 100 + 50 + 50 = 200, against 450 if all sales are added).

Key numbers

Primary22.1%21.5%21.4%19.9%
Secondary26.0%26.1%25.8%25.8%
Tertiary51.9%52.4%52.8%54.3%

MoSPI provisional estimates, base 2022-23, released 5 June 2026.

PrimarySecondaryTertiary
Share of GVA, 2025-2619.9%25.8%54.3%

Within primary in 2025-26: agriculture, livestock, forestry and fishing 18.0%; mining 1.9%. Hardin 1968; Jensen and Miller 2008 (Giffen behaviour for rice, Hunan, China).

Comparison

Non-excludableCommon pool: high-seas fish, groundwaterPublic: defence, street lights, clean air

Quick recall

  1. Sugar bought by a sweet shop: final or intermediate?
    Show answer

    intermediate.

  2. Gross investment is Rs 500 crore and depreciation Rs 120 crore. What is net investment?
    Show answer

    Rs 380 crore (500 − 120).

  3. Which class of good is non-excludable and non-rival? Give one example.
    Show answer

    a public good, e.g. national defence or street lights.

  4. Wheat sold for Rs 100, flour for Rs 150, bread for Rs 200. What is the output counted in GDP?
    Show answer

    Rs 200, the final good (value added 100 + 50 + 50).

  5. Compare services' share of GVA (2025-26) with their share of workers (2025).
    Show answer

    54.3% of GVA against 31.8% of workers.

Revision · Chapter 3Demand, Supply and Elasticity

Core idea

Demand slopes down (substitution effect, income effect, diminishing marginal utility); supply slopes up. Price settles where Qd = Qs. A change in the good's own price moves along a curve; any other determinant shifts it. Elasticity measures the size of the response, decides what happens to revenue, and decides who bears a tax.

Formulas (running example: Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = 4P − 20)

Equilibrium: 100 − 2P = 4P − 20 → P* = 20, Q* = 60.   Supply is zero at P = 5; demand is zero at P = 50.

Ed = %ΔQ / %ΔP (absolute value). Arc: (ΔQ/avg Q) / (ΔP/avg P). Point (example): Ed = 2P / Q.

Ey = %ΔQ / %Δincome.   Exy = %ΔQ of X / %ΔP of Y.   Es = %ΔQ supplied / %ΔP.

Buyers' share of a tax = Es / (Es + Ed).   CS = ½ × (50 − 20) × 60 = 900.   PS = ½ × (20 − 5) × 60 = 450.

Revision · Chapter 4Consumer Behaviour, Production and Costs

Core idea

A household divides limited income to get the most satisfaction; a firm turns inputs into output and faces costs. The demand curve comes out of the consumer's choice and the supply curve out of the firm's. The law of diminishing marginal utility, the law of variable proportions and returns to scale explain the shapes of utility, product and cost curves.

Definitions

  • Utility: satisfaction from consuming a good. TU is satisfaction from all units; MU is the extra from one more unit. TU is highest where MU = 0.
  • Law of diminishing MU: each additional unit gives less satisfaction than the last. It explains the downward-sloping demand curve.
  • Indifference curve: combinations of two goods giving equal satisfaction. Slopes down, convex to the origin, higher = more satisfaction, never cross.
  • MRS: rate at which the consumer gives up one good for another at constant satisfaction; it falls as X increases.
  • Substitution effect / income effect: a dearer good is swapped for others / the price rise cuts real income. Giffen good: income effect outweighs substitution effect, so demand slopes up.
  • Law of variable proportions: with one input varied and others fixed, MP first rises, then falls, then turns negative (short run). Returns to scale: all inputs varied together (long run).
  • Minimum efficient scale: output at which LAC is lowest. LAC is the lower envelope of the SAC curves.

Formulas

MU = change in TU from one more unit.   Consumer equilibrium: MUx / Px = MUy / Py (all income spent), or MRS = Px / Py. Budget line: M = Px·x + Py·y.

AP = TP / L.   MP = change in TP. MP cuts AP at AP's maximum.

TC = FC + VC.   ATC = TC / q = AFC + AVC.   MC = change in TC for one more unit. MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimums.

    MU = 0 (the sixth orange in the example).

  2. State the consumer equilibrium condition.
    Show answer

    MUx/Px = MUy/Py with all income spent; equivalently MRS = Px/Py.

  3. When does a Giffen good arise?
    Show answer

    when the income effect of a price rise outweighs the substitution effect, so demand slopes upward.

  4. Where does MC cut ATC?
    Show answer

    at ATC's minimum (about Rs 21.7 in the example).

  5. How does returns to scale differ from the law of variable proportions?
    Show answer

    returns to scale vary all inputs together (long run); the law varies one input with others fixed (short run).

Revision · Chapter 5Market Structures

Core idea

A market structure is the pattern of competition set by the number of sellers, the kind of product and ease of entry. Every firm maximises profit where MR = MC (with MC rising); structures differ only in what MR looks like. India regulates market power through the Competition Act, 2002, enforced by the CCI.

Definitions

  • Price taker: a perfectly competitive firm; AR = MR = price, demand is horizontal.
  • Shutdown rule: price below minimum AVC (Rs 9.75 in the example): shut down. Price between AVC and ATC: loss, but keep producing. Short-run supply = MC above minimum AVC.
  • Normal profit: return that keeps the owner in business, counted as a cost; long-run perfect competition ends at zero economic profit.
  • Deadweight loss: value of mutually beneficial trades lost because a monopolist restricts output.
  • Price discrimination: different prices for the same good, not due to cost; needs market power, separable buyers, no resale. First degree: each pays her maximum; second: by quantity (slabs); third: by group (student fares).
  • Natural monopoly: one firm serves the market cheaper than two (railway track, water pipes); regulators allow P = average cost.
  • Prisoner's dilemma / Nash equilibrium: each firm picks its best response; the result is worse than cooperation, so cartels are unstable.
  • Kinked demand: rivals match a price cut but not a rise, so oligopoly prices are sticky.

Formulas

TR = P × q.   AR = TR / q = P.   MR = extra revenue from one more unit. Profit-maximising rule: MR = MC (perfect competition: P = MC).

HHI = sum of squared market shares (%). Four firms at 25% each: 4 × 625 = 2,500; monopoly: 100² = 10,000.

Revision · Chapter 6National Income Accounting

Core idea

National income accounting measures a country's output, income and expenditure; GDP, growth, inflation and deficit ratios all rest on it. Output, income and expenditure are three views of the same total. Aggregates differ by gross vs net (depreciation) and domestic vs national (NFIA). India's current series has base year 2022-23.

Definitions

  • GDP: market value of final goods and services produced within domestic territory in a year (1 April to 31 March). Location decides, not citizenship.
  • GVA: output − intermediate consumption; adding value added at each stage avoids double counting.
  • NFIA: factor income received from abroad − factor income paid abroad. Remittances, gifts and aid are transfers: not in NFIA or GNP. India's NFIA has been negative, so GDP > GNP.
  • Valuation: factor cost → (+ production taxes − subsidies) → basic price → (+ product taxes − subsidies) → market price. Headline: GDP at market price; sectors: GVA at basic price.
  • Nominal vs real GDP: current-year prices vs base-year prices. ICOR: extra capital per unit of extra output; lower is better.
  • PPP: converts incomes using a rate equalising the price of a common basket; ranks India higher than the market exchange rate does.

Formulas

GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).   GNP = GDP + NFIA.   NDP = GDP − depreciation.   NNP = GNP − depreciation.   National income = NNP at factor cost.

GDP deflator = (nominal / real) × 100.   ICOR = investment rate / growth rate (32% and 8% give 4).

Personal income = national income − undistributed profits − corporate tax + transfers. Disposable income = personal income − personal direct taxes.

Revision · Chapter 7Growth, Development and Welfare Metrics

Core idea

Growth is a sustained rise in real output per person; development is the wider improvement in health, education and freedom. Growth is necessary but not sufficient for development, and it can be jobless, ruthless or rootless. Growth theories differ on the source of long-run growth, and the HDI and related indices judge whether lives are improving.

Definitions

  • Growth vs development: growth: quantitative rise in real GDP, measured by GDP; development: qualitative change (less poverty, illiteracy, disease), measured by HDI and similar.
  • Harrod-Domar: growth = saving rate / ICOR; raise investment and use capital efficiently.
  • Solow: saving changes the level of output per worker, not long-run growth; technology (given from outside) sets long-run growth; poor countries converge.
  • Endogenous growth (Romer, Lucas): knowledge and human capital produced within the economy; spending on education and R&D raises growth permanently.
  • Sen (Development as Freedom, 1999): development = expansion of real freedoms. Commodities (what one has), functionings (what one can be or do), capabilities (real opportunity to achieve them).
  • HDI: created 1990 by Mahbub ul Haq with Sen; published by UNDP. Geometric mean of health, education and income indices (arithmetic mean until 2010); penalises uneven development.
  • Middle-income trap: a country escapes low income through low-wage manufacturing, then stalls.

Formulas

Growth rate = (real GDP now − real GDP last year) / last year × 100. Per capita: 8% GDP and 1% population → 1.08 / 1.01 = 6.9%. Rule of 70: years to double ≈ 70 / growth rate.

Index = (actual − minimum) / (maximum − minimum). Income index = (ln GNI − ln 100) / (ln 75,000 − ln 100). HDI = cube root (health × education × income). Education index = average of the two schooling indices.

Solow: change in k = saving per worker − (n + d) × k. IHDI loss = 1 − IHDI / HDI.

Revision · Chapter 8Income Determination and the Multiplier

Core idea

Keynes (General Theory, 1936) held that output is decided by total spending (effective demand), which can fall short of full employment. In the simple model, equilibrium is where planned spending equals output (Y = AE), or planned saving equals planned investment. The multiplier turns a change in spending into a larger change in income.

Definitions

  • MPC / MPS: share of an extra rupee spent / saved; MPS = 1 − MPC. APC = C / Y falls as income rises.
  • Deflationary gap: shortfall of planned spending at full employment (40 in the example); output shortfall = gap × multiplier (40 × 5 = 200). Inflationary gap: excess spending at full employment.
  • Paradox of thrift: if all try to save more, income falls and total saving stays equal to investment.
  • MEC: rate of discount that equates the present value of expected yields to cost; invest when MEC > r.
  • Accelerator: net investment = v × change in output; it falls when output growth slows even if output still rises.
  • Say's law (classical): supply creates its own demand; markets clear; unemployment temporary. Keynesian: wages sticky, demand decides output, unemployment can persist.

Formulas

C = a + bY.   AE = C + I.   Equilibrium: Y = AE (or S = I). Example: C = 100 + 0.8Y, I = 100 → Y = 200 + 0.8Y → Y = 1,000.

Multiplier = 1 / (1 − MPC) = 1 / MPS. Tax multiplier = −b / (1 − b); balanced-budget multiplier = 1. With proportional tax: 1 / (1 − b(1 − t)); with imports: 1 / (1 − b(1 − t) + m).

I = I₀ − d × r.   I = v × ΔY. Lump-sum tax: Y = (a − bT + I + G) / (1 − b).

Revision · Chapter 9IS-LM and AD-AS

Core idea

IS-LM finds the interest rate and income at which the goods and money markets are both in equilibrium. AD-AS adds the price level to show how output and prices respond to demand and supply shocks. Fiscal and monetary policy work differently, and a liquidity trap shows when a central bank runs out of room.

Definitions

  • IS curve: combinations of r and Y with planned investment = saving; slopes down. Shifts right with higher G, lower taxes, higher autonomous C or I, higher exports.
  • LM curve: combinations of r and Y with money demand = money supply; slopes up. Shifts right with higher money supply; a higher price level shifts it left.
  • Motives for money (Keynes): transactions and precautionary (depend on income); speculative (depends on interest rate).
  • Theories of the interest rate: classical (loanable funds): the rate equates saving and investment; Keynes (liquidity preference): the rate is set by demand for and supply of money. Fisher: nominal = real + expected inflation.
  • Crowding out: government borrowing raises the interest rate and displaces private investment.
  • Liquidity trap: interest rate so low that extra money is held, not lent; LM is flat; monetary policy weak, fiscal policy fully effective.
  • AD slopes down because of: wealth effect, interest-rate effect, exchange-rate (net export) effect.
  • SRAS / LRAS: SRAS slopes up (sticky input prices); LRAS vertical at potential output.
  • Stagflation: adverse supply shock (e.g. oil) shifts SRAS left: output falls, prices rise.

Worked example (the chapter's numbers)

IS: C = 40 + 0.8Y, I = 300 − 20r, G = 60 → Y = 2,000 − 100r.   LM: L = 0.5Y − 50r, M = 400 → Y = 800 + 100r.

Equilibrium: 2,000 − 100r = 800 + 100r → r = 6, Y = 1,400.

    Show answer

  4. How do classical and Keynesian theories of interest differ?
    Show answer

    classical: saving = investment; Keynes: demand for and supply of money.

  5. When is monetary policy ineffective?
    Show answer

    in a liquidity trap (flat LM).

  6. What is stagflation, and what causes it in AD-AS?
    Show answer

    falling output with rising prices; SRAS shifts left (e.g. an oil price rise).

Revision · Chapter 10Inflation

Core idea

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. It arises from demand-pull, cost-push and structural causes, redistributes between debtors and creditors, and is measured in India by CPI (the RBI's target) and WPI. The Phillips curve links it to unemployment: a trade-off in the short run, vertical at NAIRU in the long run.

Definitions

  • Base effect: a low base last year makes a small rise this year look like high inflation; a high base does the reverse.
  • Demand-pull / cost-push / structural: excess demand at full capacity / rising input costs (oil, wages, weak rupee) / supply bottlenecks (storage, logistics, middlemen).
  • Headline vs core: headline = whole CPI basket; core = excluding food and fuel.
  • Disinflation vs deflation: inflation falls but stays positive (8% to 5%) vs the price level falls (below 0). Skewflation: a few items; shrinkflation: smaller pack at same price.
  • Stagflation: slow growth and high unemployment with high inflation; broke the stable Phillips trade-off in the 1970s.
  • NAIRU: natural rate of unemployment; long-run Phillips curve is vertical there (Friedman, Phelps).
  • Bracket creep / inflation tax: higher nominal incomes push people into higher slabs / inflation taxes money holders when a deficit is printed.
  • Essential Commodities Act, 1955: lets governments regulate trade and stock limits to prevent hoarding.

Formulas

Inflation (%) = (this year's index − last year's) / last year's × 100. Index 120 → 126 = 5%.

Fisher: nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation.   GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP × 100 (300 / 250 → 120).   Headline ≈ Σ weight × price rise (food 36.75% × 10% ≈ 3.7%).

    it has no services and records wholesale, not retail, prices (Urjit Patel Committee, 2014).

  4. What happened to food's weight in CPI in the 2024 series?
    Show answer

    fell from 45.86% to 36.75%.

  5. What is the long-run shape of the Phillips curve?
    Show answer

    vertical at NAIRU.

Revision · Chapter 11Employment, Unemployment and Labour Law

Core idea

Employment economics covers how many work, how many seek work and cannot find it, the surveys that measure this in India, and the laws and social security that govern work. India's bigger problem is underemployment and informality; 29 central labour laws were merged into four codes, in force from 21 November 2025.

Definitions

  • Unemployed: no work at the prevailing wage although able and willing; someone who cannot or does not wish to work is not unemployed.
  • Structural / cyclical / frictional: skills mismatch / fall in demand in a downturn / job-switching, present even at full employment. Natural rate = frictional + structural (NAIRU).
  • Disguised unemployment: more people work than needed; marginal productivity zero; removing some leaves output unchanged.
  • Underemployment: employed but not in the desired capacity.
  • Usual status / CWS / current daily status: principal activity of previous year (+ subsidiary: 30+ days) / at least 1 hour on 1 day in last 7 / each day of the week (1-4 hours half day, over 4 full day).
  • PLFS (NSO, MoSPI): replaced the five-yearly NSSO surveys; first annual report (July 2017 to June 2018) published May 2019. AQEES (Labour Bureau): QES for 10+ workers, AFES for 9 or fewer.
  • Labour: is on the Concurrent List.

Formulas

LF = employed + unemployed.   LFPR = LF / population (age group) × 100.   WPR = employed / population × 100.   UR = unemployed / LF × 100. Example: 600 employed, 30 unemployed, 370 outside → LF 630, LFPR 63%, WPR 60%, UR 4.76%.

Revision · Chapter 12Business Cycles

Core idea

A business cycle is the recurring rise and fall of actual output around long-run potential output. It has five phases, several named cycle lengths and many competing explanations. All five of India's recessions listed in the source were supply shocks (drought, war, oil, pandemic).

Definitions

  • Potential output: output when labour and capital are used at normal, high utilisation; grows slowly with inputs and technology.
  • Output gap: negative gap = idle resources and weak demand; positive = overheating and inflation pressure.
  • Recession: at least two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth (6 to 18 months, widespread). Depression: severe, protracted. Slowdown: growth falls but stays positive.
  • Counter-cyclical vs pro-cyclical: fiscal policy that works against / amplifies the cycle.

Formulas

Output gap = (actual GDP − potential GDP) / potential GDP × 100. Potential Rs 200 lakh crore: actual 190 → −5%; actual 206 → +3%.

Key numbers

India's recessions (negative real growth)GrowthCause
1957-58−1.2%Drought
1965-66−3.66%Drought and war
1972-73−0.32%Drought and oil crisis
1979-80−5.2%Drought and political instability
2020-21−6.6%Covid-19

Source-book figures: older years on earlier base years; the 2020-21 figure has been revised. Leading indicators: stock prices, new orders, building permits; lagging: unemployment duration, inflation, bank credit. Slowdown example: GDP 100, 108, 112, 115 → growth 8%, 3.7%, 2.7%: still a slowdown, not a recession.

    Show answer

    two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth.

    Show answer

    −5%.

  3. Which cycle is caused by fixed business investment, and how long is it?
    Show answer

    the Juglar cycle, 7 to 11 years.

  4. What kind of shocks caused all five of India's listed recessions?
    Show answer

    supply shocks (drought, war, oil, pandemic).

  5. What does a K-shaped recovery mean?
    Show answer

    different parts of the economy recover differently: some rise, others keep falling.

Revision · Chapter 13Stabilisation Policy and the Policy Mix

Core idea

Stabilisation policy uses government spending, taxation and the central bank's interest rate to keep output near potential and inflation low. Fiscal policy acts on demand directly; monetary policy acts through interest rates and credit. The right mix depends on whether the economy faces a slump, a boom, stagflation or a liquidity trap.

Definitions

  • Pump priming: government spending put into the economy to raise demand.
  • Counter-cyclical / pro-cyclical: works against / amplifies the cycle. Fiscal multipliers are larger in recessions than in expansions (Economic Survey).
  • Automatic stabilisers: taxes and transfers that move with the cycle without a new decision (falling tax revenue, MGNREGA demand rising); discretionary = deliberate change.
  • Crowding out / crowding in: government bonds displace private borrowers (strongest in a boom) / government spending pulls in private investment when resources are idle (recession).
  • IRGD: interest rate-growth rate differential; if interest rate on debt stays below growth, growth lowers the debt-to-GDP ratio.
  • Lags: recognition, decision, impact. Fiscal: long decision lag; monetary: long impact lag.
  • Supply shocks: a food-price spike is not cured by managing demand; the repo rate has limited effect.

Key numbers

IS-LM example: G up by 60 raised income by 150 instead of 300 (rate 6% to 7.5%). 2020-21: repo rate held at 4%, spending and borrowing expanded, path to fiscal deficit below 4.5% of GDP by 2025-26. 2026: inflation target 4% (2% to 6% band, 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031); repo rate raised from 5.25% to 5.50% on 7 October 2026 with CPI inflation at 5.54% in September 2026. FRBM Act: Centre may not borrow from the RBI except through ways and means advances.

Comparison

Fiscal policyMonetary policy
WhoGovernment (Finance Ministry, Parliament)RBI
ToolsSpending, taxes, borrowingRepo rate, reserve ratios, OMOs, liquidity operations
ChannelDirectly changes aggregate demandInterest rates, credit, exchange rate
SpeedSlow to legislate, fast once spending startsFast to decide, slow to affect
SituationFiscalMonetaryResult
Deep recessionExpansionaryExpansionaryStrong rise in output; no crowding out
Boom, high inflationContractionaryContractionaryDemand and inflation fall; risk of overshooting
StagflationContractionary or supply measuresContractionaryLower inflation at some cost in output
Cut deficit, keep growthContractionaryExpansionaryLower rates offset the fiscal drag
Growth with inflation controlExpansionaryContractionaryHigher rates; crowding out; exchange-rate pressure
Cycle stagePro-cyclicalCounter-cyclical

RecessionSpending down, taxes upSpending up, taxes down

Quick recall

  1. What do counter-cyclical policies do in a recession?
    Show answer

    raise spending and cut taxes.

  2. When is crowding out strongest?
    Show answer

    in a boom, when resources are fully used.

  3. When must the government use fiscal tools because monetary policy has no room?
    Show answer

    in a liquidity trap, when the policy rate nears zero and demand is weak.

  4. Which policy mix suits a deep recession?
    Show answer

    expansionary fiscal and expansionary monetary.

  5. When does growth lower the debt-to-GDP ratio?
    Show answer

    when the interest rate on debt is below the growth rate (negative IRGD).

Revision · Chapter 14Nature of Money

Core idea

Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. It replaces barter, which needs a double coincidence of wants. Rupee notes are fiat money issued by the RBI; the quantity theory links money to prices; seigniorage, demonetisation and digital money (e-Rupee) are the applied topics.

Definitions

  • Double coincidence of wants: barter works only if each party wants what the other offers.
  • Legal tender: money the law requires creditors to accept in payment of debt; a cheque is not legal tender.
  • Fiat money: money by government order, not backed by a commodity; rupee notes and coins.
  • Minimum Reserve System (1957): RBI holds gold and foreign securities worth at least Rs 200 crore (gold at least Rs 115 crore); the rest of the issue can be backed by rupee securities.
  • Seigniorage: profit from creating money: interest on assets backing currency; interest-free CRR balances; the inflation tax (inflation × monetary base).
  • e-Rupee (CBDC): legal tender issued by the RBI in digital form, 1:1 with cash, bearer instrument. Crypto: private, not legal tender, an asset (30% tax on transfer; 1% TDS, Finance Act 2022).
  • e-RUPI: a person- and purpose-specific digital voucher on UPI; not a CBDC; not transferable; not convertible to cash.

Formulas

MV = PT (for GDP: MV = PY), Fisher. Cambridge: M = kPY, k = 1/V. Example: M 500, V 4, Y 2,000 → P = Rs 1; M up 10% → P = Rs 1.10; if Y also up 10% → P stays 1.00.

e-Rupee in circulation, RBI Annual Report 2024-25about Rs 1,016 crore

    Rs 1.

    Show answer

    e-RUPI is a purpose-specific voucher, not a CBDC, and cannot be converted into cash.

Revision · Chapter 15Liquidity Aggregates

Core idea

Money supply is the stock of cash and bank deposits held by the public; cash held by the RBI, government and banks is excluded. Measures range from narrow (M1) to broad (M3, L1 to L3). The monetary base (reserve money) is central bank money; the money multiplier links it to money supply.

Definitions

  • Demand vs term deposits: demand deposits (current, savings) are withdrawable any time and cheque-able; term deposits (FD, RD) are not.
  • Legal tender: notes and coins cannot be refused for a debt; Re 1 note and coins are the Government's liability; other notes backed by assets (Section 33, RBI Act); Government guarantees under Section 26.
  • Monetary base (M0): currency with the public + vault cash + banks' deposits with the RBI (+ "other" deposits). Different from money supply.
  • Reserve money rises / falls: when the RBI buys / sells foreign exchange or government securities. Tax collection lowers money supply and reserve money; spending restores them.
  • Fractional reserve banking: banks keep a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest, so a given base supports more money.

Formulas

cdr = currency / deposits.   rdr = reserves / deposits (CRR + SLR + excess).

Money multiplier = M / H = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr). cdr 1, rdr 0.2 → 5/3. cdr 0.2, rdr 0.1 → 4 (Rs 100 crore supports Rs 400 crore); rdr 0.2 → 3.

Key numbers
