Revision · Chapter 16The Reserve Bank of India

Core idea

The RBI is the central bank: it issues currency, runs monetary policy, regulates banks, NBFCs and payment systems, manages forex reserves, and acts as banker and debt manager to the government. Its autonomy is within limits, set by Section 7 of the RBI Act.

Definitions

  • Origin: Hilton Young Commission; RBI Act, 1934; began 1 April 1935; nationalised 1949. Board of up to 21; Governor draws powers from the Act.
  • PSBs vs private banks: PSBs: dual regulation by Centre and RBI; RBI cannot supersede their boards or revoke a licence. Private banks: RBI approval for chairman, MD and CEO; can supersede the board. Cooperative banks: dual regulation. RBI can supersede an NBFC board (July 2019 amendment).
  • DICGC: 100% RBI subsidiary; insures up to Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank (raised from Rs 1 lakh, Feb 2020); payout within 90 days of moratorium (2021 amendment).
  • Ways and Means Advances: temporary loan to Centre and states for 90 days at the repo rate; non-tradable; not for funding the deficit.
  • Lender of last resort: funds against good collateral at a penal rate to a solvent bank with a temporary liquidity problem.
  • FEMA, 1999: replaced FERA, 1973 (from June 2000); RBI regulates forex. PSS Act, 2007: only RBI-authorised operators run payment systems (NPCI: 51% owned by PSBs; UPI, IMPS, RuPay, FASTag).
  • Section 7: Centre may give the RBI written directions in the public interest after consulting the Governor; never used.
  • Surplus transfer (Section 47): Economic Capital Framework; Bimal Jalan Committee (Aug 2019): Contingency Risk Buffer 5.5% to 6.5% of balance sheet.

Key numbers

Co-lending (Nov 2020): NBFC keeps at least 20% of each loan; on-lending counts up to 5% of PSL. Lead Bank Scheme: December 1969. KCC: 1998-99; loans up to Rs 5 lakh (Budget 2025-26) at 7%, prompt repayer pays 4%. Reserves: about 90% foreign currency assets, plus SDRs and gold. 2025-26 surplus transfer: about Rs 2.87 lakh crore (May 2026), buffer 6.5%. Governor, October 2026: Sanjay Malhotra.

Revision · Chapter 17Monetary Policy and Inflation Targeting

Core idea

Monetary policy is the RBI's control of money supply and interest rates to keep inflation near target while supporting growth. India uses flexible inflation targeting: 4% CPI (Combined) with a 2% to 6% band, with the Monetary Policy Committee deciding the repo rate.

Definitions

  • Framework (Feb 2015; Section 45ZA): price stability primary, growth in mind; target set every five years by Government with RBI; failure = above 6% or below 2% for three consecutive quarters (RBI reports to Government). 4% with 2% to 6% band for 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031.
  • MPC (Sept 2016; Section 45ZB): 6 members (3 RBI incl. Governor, 3 Government); Governor has casting vote; at least 4 meetings a year (RBI holds 6); binding on RBI; decides only the repo rate; exchange rate not a consideration.
  • LAF: repo, reverse repo, SDF, MSF; corridor = SDF (floor) to MSF (ceiling), repo in the middle.
  • CRR / SLR: share of NDTL kept as cash with RBI (Section 42(1), RBI Act; no interest) / kept by banks daily in government securities, gold, cash (Section 24, BR Act; ceiling 40%).
  • OMO, MSS, sterilisation: RBI buys or sells government securities (outright OMOs permanent); MSS (2004) issues T-bills for absorption, proceeds in a separate account; carrying cost borne by the budget.
  • LTRO / TLTRO / VRRR: term repo at or above repo / sector-targeted / variable-rate reverse repo to absorb liquidity.
  • Liquidity trap: repo rate near zero, cuts no longer revive demand; fiscal policy must act.

Formulas

Corridor: SDF = repo − 0.25%; MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 0.25%. October 2026: repo 5.50%, SDF 5.25%, MSF and Bank Rate 5.75% (corridor 50 bp). EBLR: home loan = repo + spread (5.50% + 3% = 8.50%; repo 5.75% → 8.75%).

NDTL Rs 1,000 crore, CRR 3%, SLR 18%: Rs 30 crore with RBI, Rs 180 crore in securities, Rs 790 crore available. Nominal rate = inflation + real rate.

Revision · Chapter 18Banking Architecture

Core idea

Banking architecture is the structure of banks and other financial institutions that collect savings and lend them, and the regulators above them. Indian banking moved from presidency banks to nationalisation (1969, 1980) to reform (Narasimhan committees), and now has public, private, foreign, rural, small finance, payments and cooperative banks beside NBFIs.

Definitions

  • Milestones: presidency banks: Bengal 1806, Bombay 1840, Madras 1843; Imperial Bank 1921; SBI 1955; 14 banks nationalised 19 July 1969 (deposits above Rs 50 crore); 6 more April 1980 (above Rs 200 crore); public share of deposits 92%; PSL target 33.3% → 40%.
  • Bank vs NBFI: a bank accepts demand deposits and issues cheques on itself; an NBFI does not.
  • Scheduled bank: included in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934; keeps reserves with RBI under that Act.
  • RRBs: set up 1975 (RRB Act, 1976); ownership Centre : state : sponsor bank = 50 : 15 : 35; 75% priority sector; supervised by NABARD.
  • SFBs / payments banks: SFB licences to 10 (Sept 2015): 75% priority sector, at least 50% loans up to Rs 25 lakh. Payments banks licences to 11 (Aug 2015): deposits up to Rs 2 lakh; cannot lend or issue credit cards.
  • Cooperative banks: banking laws extended 1966; dual control (RBI banking functions; RCS / CRCS management). Three tiers short-term: StCB, DCCB, PACS (outside the BR Act); long-term: SCARDB, PCARDB.
  • NBFC: needs an RBI certificate of registration; principal business not agriculture, industry, trade or real estate. CICs (four): TransUnion CIBIL, Equifax, Experian, CRIF High Mark.
  • FSDC: set up December 2010; non-statutory; chaired by the Finance Minister.

Revision · Chapter 19Capital Adequacy, NPAs and IBC

Core idea

Capital adequacy is the cushion of own funds a bank holds against loan losses; the NPA framework identifies bad loans; SARFAESI, ARCs, NARCL and the IBC (2016) are the tools to recover or resolve them. Gross NPA of scheduled commercial banks fell to 1.8% in March 2026.

Definitions

  • CAR / CRAR: capital as % of risk-weighted assets. Tier 1 (going-concern; CET1 core): equity and disclosed reserves. Tier 2 (gone-concern): revaluation reserves, general provisions, subordinated debt. Set by the RBI, not the bank.
  • PCA: RBI early-warning framework; triggers: capital, asset quality (net NPA), leverage; curbs on dividends, branches, lending. Not for RRBs, payments banks, SFBs (UCBs and RRBs: Supervisory Action Framework).
  • D-SIB: assets above 2% of GDP; SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank; extra capital. D-SIIs (2020-21): LIC, GIC Re, New India Assurance.
  • NPA: principal or interest overdue for more than 90 days. Stressed assets = NPAs + restructured + written-off. Write-off removes the loan from the balance sheet; the borrower still owes. Net NPA = gross NPA − provisions.
  • SARFAESI Act, 2002: 60-day notice; enforce security without court; ARCs (RBI-regulated); securitisation.
  • NARCL (2021, "bad bank"): 51% public sector banks and institutions, 49% private lenders; buys stressed loans; IDRCL resolves. A Rs 1,000 crore NPA sold at Rs 300 crore: 15% cash (Rs 45 crore) + 85% security receipts (Rs 255 crore), Government-guaranteed.
  • IBC (enacted May 2016): shifts control to creditors on default; NCLT for companies (appeal NCLAT), DRT for individuals (DRAT).

Formulas

CAR = (Tier 1 + Tier 2) / RWA. Capital 1, RWA 2.5 → 40%; RWA 3.5 → about 29%. India: 11.5% (Tier 1 7% + Tier 2 2% + CCB 2.5%).

Revision · Chapter 20Financial Markets and Government Securities

Core idea

A financial market trades instruments such as shares, bonds and short-term paper. The money market deals in instruments up to one year and the capital market in those above one year. Government securities are the risk-free benchmark, and bond prices move opposite to interest rates.

Definitions

  • Equity vs debt: equity: part ownership, variable return, voting rights; debt: money lent, fixed coupon plus principal, no control.
  • Bond price and rates: move in opposite directions. Rs 100 bond at 10%; bought at Rs 80 yields 10/80 = 12.5%. An RBI rate hike lowers the value of banks' bond holdings.
  • Company types: government company: at least 51% public ownership; private company: up to 200 members; public company: not private; IPO lists a private company publicly.
  • Primary vs secondary market: securities sold first time (money to issuer) vs traded between investors (no money to issuer).
  • G-sec: tradable debt of Centre or State; virtually no default risk (gilt-edged); all four types count towards SLR. Sold by RBI auctions on E-Kuber; traded on NDS-OM.
  • Retail Direct Scheme (Nov 2021): individuals open a Retail Direct Gilt account with the RBI; non-competitive window only.
  • FAR (March 2020): Fully Accessible Route: no investment ceiling for non-residents in specified G-secs.
  • Corporate bond market: slow because of governance gaps, costly public issues (firms prefer bank loans or private placement), earlier weak bankruptcy law; backstop facility in Budget 2021-22.

Commercial Paper7 days to one year; unsecured promissory note
Repo / reverse repo, TREPSSecured against government securities

T-bill example: 91-day Rs 100 bill issued at Rs 98.20 earns Rs 1.80. FPI limit in corporate bonds raised to 15% of outstanding stock (from 9%). Repo rate 5.50% from 7 October 2026.

Revision · Chapter 21Capital Markets

Core idea

The capital market is where long-term funds are raised and traded through shares and bonds. SEBI, set up in 1988 and statutory since April 1992, regulates it. Companies raise money through IPOs, FPOs, rights issues and placements; derivatives and funds (AIFs, REITs, InvITs) add instruments.

Definitions

  • IPO / FPO / OFS: unlisted company offers shares to the public first time / listed company issues more / existing holders sell and the company gets no money (used for disinvestment).
  • Rights issue / QIP / bonus: new shares first to existing holders / placement to institutional buyers by a listed company / free shares out of reserves.
  • Anchor investor: introduced by SEBI in 2009; institution subscribing before the IPO opens. Book building: price band, bids set the price.
  • SEBI: set up 1988; statutory April 1992 (SEBI Act); Capital Issues Control Act repealed May 1992; aims: protect investors, develop and regulate the market; appeals to SAT.
  • IPO quotas; listing: QIB up to 50%, NII at least 15%, retail (up to Rs 2 lakh) at least 35%; listing in T+3; minimum public shareholding 25%. NSDL and CDSL hold shares in demat form.
  • Investor protection: open offer for at least 26% when an acquirer crosses 25% (SAST 2011); no trading on UPSI (PIT 2015); market-wide circuit breakers at 10%, 15%, 20%; FMC merged into SEBI in 2015.
  • Mutual fund: sponsor, trustees, AMC, custodian; NAV = (assets − liabilities) / units; ELSS has a 3-year lock-in.
  • AIF: privately pooled fund for sophisticated investors (VC, PE, hedge funds); angel investors regulated under AIF rules. NIIF (2015): Category II AIF, Government stake 49%.
  • REITs / InvITs: SEBI-regulated trusts under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882; own real estate / infrastructure; at least 80% of assets in revenue-generating projects.
  • ADR / GDR: receipt issued by an overseas depository against shares held by a domestic custodian; one receipt can represent a bundle of shares.
  • Derivatives: contract whose value depends on an underlying; used for hedging, speculation, arbitrage. SEBI regulates exchange-traded; RBI regulates OTC interest-rate and currency derivatives.

Revision · Chapter 22Financial Inclusion

Core idea

Financial inclusion is the delivery of affordable accounts, credit, insurance, pensions and payments to every section of society, especially the poor. India's route runs through RRBs (1975), PMJDY (August 2014), payments and small finance banks, the JAM trinity for direct benefit transfers, UPI, and consent-based data sharing.

Definitions

  • PMJDY (Aug 2014): zero-balance basic account; RuPay debit card with accident insurance; overdraft; DBT.
  • JAM trinity: Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + mobile numbers: lets subsidies move by DBT and ends leakages.
  • NSFI 2019-24 (RBI): six pillars: universal access; basic bouquet of services; livelihood and skill development; financial literacy; customer protection and grievance redressal; effective coordination.
  • Payments banks / SFBs: payments banks (licensed Aug 2015): no lending, no credit cards, demand deposits only. SFBs (Sept 2015): 75% priority sector credit, at least 50% of loans up to Rs 25 lakh.
  • CICs (2005 Act): TransUnion CIBIL, Equifax, Experian, CRIF High Mark.
  • NPCI: umbrella body for retail payments; launched RuPay and UPI.
  • RB-IOS (12 Nov 2021): merged three ombudsman schemes; complain to the entity first, to the Ombudsman after 30 days; compensation up to Rs 20 lakh (loss) plus Rs 1 lakh (harassment); appeal to the RBI Executive Director.
  • Account Aggregator: RBI-regulated NBFC-AA (Directions of 2 Sept 2016); moves financial data only with consent, does not store or read it. FIP provides data; FIU uses it.
  • Digital Lending Directions (8 May 2025): lender accountable for lending service providers; Key Fact Statement; cooling-off period; direct fund flow (no LSP pass-through account); data stored in India; grievance officer.

Revision · Chapter 23Financial Products: Insurance, Savings and Gold Schemes

Core idea

Financial products let households protect against risk, save and hold wealth. Insurance pools risk; small savings feed the National Small Savings Fund with rates reset quarterly; the Sovereign Gold Bond and Gold Monetisation schemes aim to bring idle household gold into the economy and reduce gold imports.

Definitions

  • Insurance: pools risk: many pay small premiums, the insurer pays a large sum to the few who suffer loss. Life: fixed sum on death (or maturity); general: fire, marine, motor, home, health, crop.
  • Penetration / density: premium as % of GDP (Economic Survey 2020-21: life 2.82%, non-life 0.94%) / premium per head in US$ (life 58.0, non-life 19).
  • NSSF: National Small Savings Fund (public account) holds PPF, KVP, Sukanya Samriddhi, NSC and post office deposits; lends to Centre and States; rates reset every quarter, linked to G-sec yields. High small-savings rates hold back deposit-rate cuts.
  • Sovereign Gold Bond (Nov 2015): G-sec denominated in grams of gold, issued by the RBI for the Government; fixed interest plus gold price at redemption; counted in market borrowing.
  • Gold Monetisation Scheme (Nov 2015): households and institutions deposit gold with banks and earn interest; banks can lend it to jewellers.
  • Purpose of SGB and GMS: bring idle household gold into the economy and cut gold imports; not to promote FDI in gold (UPSC 2016).

Revision · Chapter 24Tax Theory

Core idea

A tax is a compulsory payment to the government with no specific, direct return. Tax theory covers the purposes and canons of taxation, progressive, proportional and regressive rates, direct and indirect taxes, who really bears a tax, buoyancy, the Laffer curve, and how VAT removes cascading through input tax credit.

Definitions

  • Smith's canons (1776): equality, certainty, convenience, economy. Good tax system: fair, efficient, flexible (elastic, buoyant), simple.
  • Progressive / proportional / regressive: rate rises with income / same rate / rate falls with income. All indirect taxes tend to be regressive. Marginal rate is above the average rate in a progressive tax.
  • Specific vs ad valorem: fixed amount per unit (Rs 5 per litre) vs percentage of value (18%).
  • Direct vs indirect: impact and incidence on the same person vs impact on seller, incidence on consumer. Direct: income, corporate, property; indirect: GST, customs, excise.
  • Origin vs destination: CST was origin-based; GST is destination-based (revenue to the consuming state).
  • Tax incidence: the less elastic side bears more; a tax creates deadweight loss.
  • Laffer curve: revenue zero at 0% and 100%; rises to a maximum at some rate, then falls (evasion, discouraged work and saving).
  • Tax expenditure: revenue forgone through exemptions and concessions, published with the Budget.
  • Cascading / VAT: sales tax at each stage taxes the same value repeatedly; VAT taxes value added, and input tax credit removes cascading. VAT: multi-point, destination-based tax on final consumption.

Formulas

Tax buoyancy = % change in tax revenue / % change in nominal GDP (includes rate changes; above 1 is good). Tax elasticity = same with rates and exemptions unchanged. GDP +10%, revenue +12% → 1.2; revenue +8% → 0.8.

Tax-GDP ratio = tax revenue / GDP × 100.   Average rate = tax / income; marginal rate = rate on next rupee.

Key numbers

Illustrative slabs (nil to 3 lakh; 10% 3-6 lakh; 20% above)Result
Income Rs 8 lakh10% × 3 lakh = 30,000 + 20% × 2 lakh = 40,000 = Rs 70,000; average 8.75%; marginal 20%
VAT at 10%Seller ASeller B (buys from A)
Input cost0Rs 110 (A's price incl. VAT)
Value added; sale priceRs 100; Rs 100Rs 200; Rs 300
VAT charged / paid to governmentRs 10 / Rs 10Rs 30 / Rs 30 − 10 credit = Rs 20
Total tax to governmentRs 30 = 10% of final price Rs 300Consumer pays Rs 330

Centre's tax-GDP ratio (before devolution; Business Standard analysis): 11.5% in April-September 2024 with buoyancy 1.3; 10.8% in April-September 2025 with buoyancy 0.32 (half-year figures only). Bread tax Rs 5: 0.0005% of Rs 10 lakh income vs 0.005% of Rs 1 lakh.

Quick recall

    Show answer

    equality, certainty, convenience, economy.

  2. Nominal GDP grows 10% and tax revenue 12%. What is buoyancy?
    Show answer

    1.2.

  3. Why does input tax credit matter?
    Show answer

    it removes the cascading effect and discourages evasion, since each seller asks for a receipt from the one before.

  4. Is CST origin-based or destination-based?
    Show answer

    origin-based (GST is destination-based).

  5. What does the Laffer curve say about a 100% tax rate?
    Show answer

    revenue is zero.

Revision · Chapter 25The Union Budget

Core idea

The Union Budget is the Annual Financial Statement (Article 112) that Parliament must approve before any tax is levied or money spent. It is passed through the Appropriation Bill and Finance Bill (both Money Bills), recorded in three funds, and classified into revenue and capital accounts. The 2026-27 Budget was presented on 1 February 2026.

Definitions

  • Articles: 265: no tax without law; 266: Consolidated Fund and Public Account; 267: Contingency Fund; 110: Money Bill; 112: Annual Financial Statement; 113: Demands for Grants; 114: Appropriation Bill; 116: vote on account.
  • BE / RE / actuals: next year (2026-27) / current year (2025-26) / last completed year (2024-25).
  • Interim Budget / vote on account: election-year statement covering part of the year (convention) / advance money, expenditure side only, normally two months at one-sixth of annual expenditure.
  • Guillotine: Speaker puts all remaining demands to the vote together on the last allotted day. Rajya Sabha only discusses, does not vote on demands.
  • Finance Bill: taxes; passed within 75 days (Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 2023). If Lok Sabha defeats the Budget, the Council of Ministers must resign.
  • Charged expenditure: discussed, not voted: President's emoluments; judges and CAG salaries; debt servicing; court decrees.
  • Supplementary / excess grants: amount insufficient or new service (before year end) / spent beyond grant (after year, after CAG and PAC).
  • Disinvestment: sale of Government stake; non-debt capital receipt; DIPAM is nodal; strategic disinvestment transfers management control; four strategic sectors keep a bare minimum of PSEs.
  • Gender budget (since 2005-06): Part A: 100% for women; Part B: at least 30%.

Revision · Chapter 26Deficits, Debt and the FRBM Act

Core idea

The fiscal deficit is the amount the government must borrow in a year; the revenue deficit shows how much of that borrowing finances current spending. The FRBM Act, 2003 limits deficits and debt, and the debt anchor has replaced annual deficit targets in practice. Debt has internal, external, public account and off-budget parts.

Definitions

  • Fiscal deficit = borrowing: total expenditure − receipts excluding borrowing. Equals borrowing from home + RBI + abroad.
  • Effective measures: grants to States for creating assets are revenue expenditure for the Centre but build assets; effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit − such grants; effective capital expenditure = capital expenditure + such grants.
  • Monetisation: before 1997 ad hoc T-bills to the RBI, which printed money; stopped in 1997 (replaced by WMA). FRBM prohibits direct monetisation, except in emergencies.
  • FRBM Act, 2003 (effective July 2004): E.A.S. Sharma committee (2000) draft; objectives: inter-generational equity, macro stability. Escape clause: up to 0.5% of GDP deviation. Upswing: cut deficit by at least 0.25%. Statements laid with the Budget.
  • Constitution: Article 292: Centre borrows within limits; Article 293: States borrow only internally; consent needed if they owe the Centre or it guaranteed the loan.
  • Debt components: internal (T-bills, dated securities); external (World Bank, ADB, etc.); public account liabilities (small savings, PPF); off-budget liabilities. Internal + external = public debt (about 90% of total).
  • Fiscal council: independent agency assessing fiscal plans; recommended by 14th Finance Commission and N. K. Singh Committee; about 50 countries have one.

Formulas

Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.   Fiscal deficit = (revenue + capital expenditure) − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).   Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest.

Fiscal deficit = revenue deficit + capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts. Expenditure Rs 17 lakh crore, non-borrowing receipts Rs 13 lakh crore → borrowing Rs 4 lakh crore.

Revision · Chapter 27Taxation Architecture

Core idea

The Constitution divides taxing power between the Union and the States (Seventh Schedule; Articles 268 to 272, 246A, 269A). Direct taxes cover personal and corporate income, capital gains and anti-avoidance rules; pre-GST indirect taxes cascaded. The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026.

Definitions

  • Who levies: Union: income tax (non-agricultural), corporation tax, customs, Central excise, CGST, IGST. States: land revenue, State excise on alcohol, stamp duty, SGST, agricultural income tax, professional tax (cap Rs 2,500), electricity duty. Local: property tax. Both (Art. 246A): GST.
  • Sharing: Art. 268: levied by Union, collected and kept by States; 269: assigned to States where levied; 269A: IGST apportioned by GST Council; 270: shared via Finance Commission (divisible pool); 271: surcharges kept by Union.
  • MAT: Finance Act, 1987; company pays the higher of normal tax and MAT on book profit; not for the 25.17% regime. Budget 2026-27: rate cut 15% → 14%; credit accumulation stops from 1 April 2026; AMT 15% for LLPs.
  • Equalisation Levy: 6% on online ad payments (2016); 2% on e-commerce (2020). 2% abolished from 1 Aug 2024; 6% from 1 April 2025.
  • OECD two pillars: Pillar One: reallocate taxing rights to market countries; Pillar Two: 15% minimum corporate tax.
  • Arm's length / APA / BEPS: related-party prices at market rate; Advance Pricing Agreement fixes prices in advance; BEPS = profit shifting (MLI signed June 2017, ratified June 2019).
  • GAAR / PoEM / angel tax: from 1 April 2017 (Shome Committee) / foreign company resident if key decisions made in India / abolished in Budget 2024-25.
  • Pre-GST cascading: excise 12.5% on 100 = 12.5; VAT 10% on 112.5 = 11.25; invoice 123.75; effective rate 23.75%.

Formulas and worked cases

Worked case (new regime): salary Rs 15.75 lakh − Rs 75,000 standard deduction = Rs 15 lakh. Tax 20,000 + 40,000 + 45,000 = Rs 1,05,000; cess 4% = Rs 4,200; total Rs 1,09,200 (average 7.3%, marginal 15%). Rebate (Section 87A, Rs 60,000) makes tax nil up to Rs 12 lakh (Rs 12.75 lakh salaried). Old regime rebate Rs 12,500 (nil up to Rs 5 lakh). Surcharge cap 25% (new), 37% (old).

MAT example: book profit Rs 40 lakh × 17.16% = Rs 6,86,400 beats normal tax 34.94% × Rs 15 lakh = Rs 5,24,100; company pays Rs 6,86,400.

Revision · Chapter 28Goods and Services Tax

Core idea

GST is a single, destination-based tax on the supply of goods and services, charged at every stage on value added with credit for tax paid on inputs. It began on 1 July 2017 under the 101st Constitution Amendment, is governed by the GST Council, and since 22 September 2025 has two main rates, 5% and 18%, plus 40% on luxury and sin goods.

Definitions

  • Constitution: 101st Amendment (Sept 2016): Article 246A (concurrent power), 269A (IGST), 279A (GST Council), 366(12A) (definition; alcohol for human consumption excluded). 17 taxes subsumed.
  • Not in GST: basic customs duty; alcohol (State excise); petroleum products (until Council decides, Art. 279A(5)); electricity duty; stamp duty.
  • Dual GST: within a State: CGST + SGST (UTGST in UTs); inter-State: IGST (= CGST + SGST); imports: customs duty then IGST; exports and SEZ supplies zero-rated (refund).
  • Credit use: IGST pays IGST, then CGST, then SGST. CGST pays CGST, then IGST (never SGST). SGST pays SGST, then IGST (never CGST).
  • GST Council: Union FM (chair), MoS Revenue, State ministers (Vice-Chair from States); quorum 50%; decisions need 3/4 of weighted votes: Centre 1/3, States 2/3, so Centre has a veto. Supreme Court (May 2022): recommendations are not binding.
  • Compensation (Act 2017): Centre promised to make up State shortfall below 14% a year growth over base 2015-16, for five years (1 July 2017 to 30 June 2022), funded by compensation cess; Covid loans repaid from cess until 31 March 2026.
  • Inverted duty / RoDTEP: input rate above output rate, credit piles up / refund of embedded taxes on exports in customs ledger (all exports from 1 Jan 2021; replaced MEIS).
  • Features: composition levy 1% (traders, up to Rs 1.5 crore), 6% (small services, up to Rs 50 lakh), no ITC; e-way bill above Rs 50,000; GSTIN 15 characters (state code + PAN + 3); reverse charge: buyer pays.

Revision · Chapter 29Fiscal Federalism and the Finance Commission

Core idea

Fiscal federalism is the division of taxing and spending powers between the Union and the States. The Finance Commission (Article 280) shares the Centre's tax revenue (the divisible pool) among States and recommends grants. The 16th Finance Commission (chair Arvind Panagariya) covers 2026-31 and keeps the States' share at 41%.

Definitions

  • Vertical / horizontal imbalance: Centre holds the productive taxes while States carry most spending / States differ in income and cost of services. The FC addresses both; it aims to narrow gaps, not reward the best State.
  • Divisible pool: gross tax revenue of the Centre less collection cost, cesses and surcharges (Art. 271), UT taxes, and the National Calamity Contingency Duty. Cesses and surcharges outside the pool shrink what is shared.
  • Finance Commission: Art. 280; President appoints every five years; chairman + four members; civil-court powers; report laid before Parliament with memorandum (Art. 281); recommendations advisory.
  • Functions: vertical and horizontal devolution; grants-in-aid (Art. 275); measures to supplement Panchayats and Municipalities (on SFC recommendations); other matters referred.
  • Art. 275 vs Art. 282 grants: statutory, recommended by FC, charged on the Consolidated Fund / discretionary, for any public purpose; route for Centrally Sponsored Schemes (political bias possible).
  • State borrowing: Art. 293: only in India; Centre's consent if State owes it a loan. 3% of GSDP ceiling (+0.5% for power reforms in 2023-24); March 2022: off-budget borrowing serviced from the State budget counts.

Revision · Chapter 30Trade Theory

Core idea

Countries trade because costs differ, because scale lowers cost and because consumers value variety. Comparative advantage (lower opportunity cost) is the basis of gains from trade. Tariffs protect producers but cost consumers two welfare triangles; regional integration runs from a preferential area to an economic union.

Definitions

  • Absolute vs comparative advantage: Smith: fewer resources per unit / Ricardo: lower opportunity cost; trade is beneficial if opportunity costs differ (assumes one factor, constant costs, no transport costs).
  • Heckscher-Ohlin: a country exports the good using intensively its abundant factor. Stolper-Samuelson: trade raises the return to the abundant factor, lowers the scarce one. Leontief paradox: US exports less capital-intensive than imports.
  • Product life cycle (Vernon); new trade theory (Krugman); gravity: new product at home, then exported, then production moves / scale and differentiation give intra-industry trade / trade rises with the GDP of both and falls with distance.
  • Terms of trade: net barter = export price index / import price index × 100; income = net barter × export volume index; single factoral = net barter × export productivity. Prebisch-Singer: primary prices fall relative to manufactures.
  • Tariff vs quota: tariff: domestic price rises, producers gain, consumers lose, government revenue, two triangles lost. Quota: same price effect; gain goes to licence holders.
  • Dumping: exporting below the domestic price or cost of production.
  • Trade creation vs diversion (Viner): imports from a partner replace dearer domestic production / imports shift from cheaper outsider to a dearer partner; a customs union helps only if creation exceeds diversion.

Formulas

Worked example: A makes 10 cloth or 5 wine a day; B makes 6 cloth or 6 wine. Opportunity cost of 1 cloth: A 0.5 wine, B 1 wine → A has the comparative advantage in cloth, B in wine (A is better at both goods). Any ratio between 1 wine = 1 cloth and 1 wine = 2 cloth makes both better off.

Key numbers

Stage of integrationFeatures
Preferential trade areaLower tariffs on some goods
Free trade areaNo tariffs among members; own tariff on outsiders
Customs unionFTA + common external tariff
Common marketCustoms union + free movement of labour and capital
Economic unionCommon market + common macro and exchange rate policy (EU; single currency = monetary union)
Argument for protectionComment
Infant industry (Mill-Bastable)Works only if protection is temporary
Optimal tariffLarge country lowers world price of imports; partners retaliate
National security; anti-dumping; employmentDefence, food, energy; offsets sales below home price; saves jobs at cost to consumers

Quick recall

  1. Who proposed comparative advantage?
    Show answer

    David Ricardo.

  2. In the example, who has the comparative advantage in cloth?
    Show answer

    Country A (cost 0.5 wine against B's 1 wine).

  3. What does the Leontief paradox show?
    Show answer

    US exports were less capital-intensive than its imports, contrary to Heckscher-Ohlin.

  4. How do a tariff and a quota differ?
    Show answer

    a tariff earns revenue for the government; a quota's gain goes to import licence holders.

  5. What is a customs union?
    Show answer

    a free trade area with a common external tariff.

Revision · Chapter 31Balance of Payments

Core idea

The balance of payments records all transactions between residents and non-residents in a year; it balances in accounting terms. The current account holds goods, services, primary and secondary income; the financial account holds FDI, FPI, other investment and reserves. India runs a large goods deficit financed by services and remittances.

Definitions

  • Current vs financial account test: income and transfers (no change in assets or liabilities) = current; changes in assets or liabilities = financial. Buying shares abroad: financial; dividend on them: current; foreign loan: financial; interest paid: current; gift: current.
  • Capital account (current IMF format): capital transfers and non-produced, non-financial assets; small. Older Indian wording: "capital account" meant all investment and loan items.
  • Remittances: from a non-resident (abroad over a year, intending to stay) to family: secondary income. A resident paid by a foreign firm for short work: primary income.
  • Autonomous vs accommodating: trade, investment, remittances / reserve movements financing the gap. Overall BoP = current + financial (excluding reserves) = change in reserves.
  • Balance of trade vs BoP: trade: goods only; current account adds services, primary and secondary income; BoP adds capital flows.
  • Marshall-Lerner / J-curve: depreciation improves the trade balance only if the sum of elasticities exceeds one; balance first worsens, then improves.
  • Import cover: reserves / monthly imports; reserves US$600 bn, imports US$60 bn a month → 10 months. Reserves US$726.0 bn on 9 October 2026.

Formulas

Current + capital and financial + errors and omissions = 0. Example: reserves 650; current −100, financial +150 → overall +50 → reserves 700 (valuation also moves reserves).

Revision · Chapter 32Forex, NEER, REER and Convertibility

Core idea

The exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. The rupee has been a managed float since 1993. NEER and REER measure the rupee against a basket; reserves are held by the RBI; convertibility is full on the current account and partial on the capital account.

Definitions

  • Depreciation vs devaluation: market-driven fall in the rupee / decision of the authority under a fixed or pegged rate. Appreciation vs revaluation likewise.
  • PPP idea: over the long run the exchange rate offsets the inflation difference.
  • Exchange rate systems: gold standard (to 1914); fixed (Bretton Woods, 1944 to 1971-73); fixed and adjustable (India 1947-93); free float (US, Japan, euro area); managed float (India since 1993); currency board (Hong Kong).
  • Impossible trinity: fixed rate, free capital mobility, independent monetary policy: any two. India: managed float, partial capital controls, inflation targeting.
  • NEER / REER: trade-weighted average rate against a basket / NEER adjusted for relative prices. Rising REER = real appreciation, less competitive. 40- and 6-currency indices, base 2015-16 = 100.
  • RTP: reserve tranche position: part of India's IMF quota (usually 25%) drawn without conditions.
  • Central bank swap / RBI forex swap: currencies exchanged at a fixed rate, no market risk (India-Japan 2018: US$75 bn) / RBI buys dollars now, sells back later at a higher rate; injects rupee liquidity (March 2019).
  • Convertibility: current account: free (Article VIII, IMF; 1993-94). Capital account: partial. FAR (March 2020); LRS: US$250,000 per resident individual a year.

Formulas

REER = NEER × (Indian price index ÷ partner price index). Reserves = foreign currency assets + gold + SDRs + RTP.

Revision · Chapter 33Trade Policy

Core idea

Trade policy is the set of tariffs, export incentives, remedies and agreements through which a government manages exports and imports. The DGFT administers the Foreign Trade Policy; exports are zero-rated under GST; RoDTEP replaced MEIS; SEZs and a wave of FTAs shape India's trade.

Definitions

  • DGFT / FTP: administers the Foreign Trade Policy under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992. Principles: WTO-compatible incentives; do not export taxes; duty-free imports of export inputs.
  • FTP 2023: from 1 April 2023; no end date; target US$ 2 trillion exports by 2030; four pillars; EPCG: zero duty on capital goods against an export obligation of 6 times the duty saved; Advance Authorisation for inputs.
  • Factoring / forfaiting; LC: factoring: short-term receivables sold, with or without recourse (Factoring Regulation Act 2011, amended 2021); forfaiting: medium-term export bills sold without recourse; LC follows UCP 600; collection by D/P or D/A; ECGC insures exporters.
  • RoDTEP (from 1 Jan 2021): refunds embedded taxes outside GST (fuel VAT, mandi tax, electricity duty) as credit in the customs ledger; replaced MEIS (WTO ruled MEIS non-compliant).
  • Export Promotion Mission: Cabinet 12 Nov 2025; Rs 25,060 crore over six years; Niryat Protsahan (credit) and Niryat Disha (quality, markets, infrastructure).
  • SEZ Act, 2005 (in force Feb 2006): duty-free enclave treated as foreign territory; DTA to SEZ = export; unit must be positive net foreign exchange earner over five years; supplies zero-rated. CAG: fell short; DESH proposed to replace.
  • Remedies: anti-dumping (country-specific; price below home price or cost); countervailing (country-specific; subsidy); safeguard (all sources; import surge; temporary). DGTR investigates.
  • Inverted duty structure: duty on inputs above duty on finished goods.
  • RCEP: India withdrew November 2019: trade deficit and dumping risk (China), weak rules of origin, dairy, no auto-trigger, base year 2014 refused, limited services access.
  • ITA: India joined 1996 (effective 1 July 1997): zero duty on 217 IT products by 1 Jan 2005; declined ITA-II.

Revision · Chapter 34FDI and FPI

Core idea

Foreign investment is the purchase of Indian capital instruments by non-residents. Investment of 10% or more is FDI (long-term, new capital, control); under 10% of a listed company is FPI (secondary market, volatile). India's gross FDI is high, but net FDI is small after repatriation and outward investment.

Definitions

  • FDI vs FPI test: FDI: unlisted company, or 10% or more of a listed company's paid-up equity; FPI: under 10%. Crossing 10% within a year makes it FDI. Once FDI, always FDI. An investor holds under one route per company.
  • Routes: automatic (no approval; over 95% of FDI) vs government approval route (restricted sectors; DPIIT sets policy through press notes). FPIs register with SEBI; ODI = Indian companies investing abroad.
  • ADR / GDR; ECB; Masala bond: depository receipts issued abroad / commercial loans from non-residents (incl. FCCB) / rupee-denominated ECB: investor bears the currency risk (Rs 70 bond at $1 = Rs 70; rupee at 80 repays $0.875).
  • E-commerce: 100% FDI in the marketplace model; none in the inventory model (Dec 2019 rules on vendors and exclusivity).
  • Press Note 3 (2020): approval needed for investment from land-border countries; March 2026 eased: non-controlling beneficial ownership up to 10% on automatic route in selected sectors (capital goods, electronic components, polysilicon and ingot-wafers); decisions in 60 days.
  • GIFT City / IFSC: first IFSC (SEZ Act 2005); foreign-currency transactions; India INX (BSE subsidiary); IFSCA set up April 2020 under IFSCA Act 2019; LRS up to US$250,000 a year.

Revision · Chapter 35International Organisations and the WTO

Core idea

The IMF, World Bank group and WTO govern international money, development finance and trade. Bretton Woods (1944) created the IMF and IBRD; GATT (1947) became the WTO on 1 January 1995. India's concerns centre on agricultural subsidies, TRIPS and the dispute settlement impasse.

Definitions

  • Bretton Woods (July 1944): 44 nations; IMF and IBRD (the "twins"); the planned ITO was never created.
  • IMF: Washington; Board of Governors highest; Executive Board of 24. Quota formula: GDP 50, openness 30, variability 15, reserves 5; decides subscription, votes, SDR share, access. Major decisions need 85%, so the US has a veto. India: quota 2.75%, votes 2.63%.
  • RTP (gold tranche): part of quota (typically 25%) drawn without conditions; counted in reserves.
  • SDR: created 1969; redefined as a basket after 1973; "paper gold"; 456 bn new SDRs Aug 2021 (India 12.57 bn). Basket: USD 43.38, EUR 29.31, CNY 12.28, JPY 7.59, GBP 7.44 (%).
  • IMF lending: short-term, conditional, policy reform, not projects: SBA, EFF, FCL, PLL; Rapid Credit Facility and Rapid Financing Instrument give quick help.
  • World Bank Group: IBRD (1944; middle-income), IDA (1960; interest-free to poorest), IFC (private sector), MIGA (1988; political-risk insurance), ICSID (investment disputes; India not a member). Lends for projects and policy, 25 to 30 years.
  • AIIB / NDB: 2016, Beijing, China largest vote 27.5% / 2015, Shanghai, US$50 bn initial capital, BRICS votes at least 55%.
  • GATT to WTO: GATT signed 23 countries, Geneva, 30 Oct 1947. Uruguay Round (Sept 1986 to April 1994), signed Marrakesh 15 April 1994; WTO from 1 January 1995.

Revision · Chapter 36Evolution of the Indian Economy

Core idea

India moved from a colonial economy (to 1947) through a controlled mixed economy (1950-1990) to the reforms of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation), and from agriculture directly to services without a manufacturing phase.

Definitions

  • Mixed economy: strong public sector, a private sector inside the plan, private property and democracy; began with IPR 1948.
  • Drain: one-way transfer of investible capital to Britain during colonial rule.
  • Hindu rate of growth: about 3.5% a year (term of Raj Krishna); broken in the 1980s at over 5.5%.
  • LPG: liberalisation removes state controls; privatisation transfers ownership or control (disinvestment); globalisation is the flow of goods, services, capital and labour across borders.
  • Disinvestment: token = minority sale; strategic = 51% or more sold. DIPAM is the nodal department.

Revision · Chapter 37Planning and NITI Aayog

Core idea

India planned through the Planning Commission (15 March 1950) and Five Year Plans until 2014; NITI Aayog (1 January 2015) replaced it as an advisory think tank with no power to allocate funds.

Definitions

  • Imperative vs indicative planning: state controls all aspects vs broad principles supporting the private sector. Indian planning: imperative in the public sector, indicative for the private; indicative from the Eighth Plan (1992-97).
  • Four objectives: growth, modernisation, self-reliance, equity.
  • Calcutta school: Mahalanobis: capital-intensive, heavy, public-sector-led industrialisation; won the argument.
  • Bombay school: Vakil and Brahmanand: labour-intensive wage goods, agriculture first.
  • Gadgil formula: from the Fourth Plan, plan assistance to states by formula; population 60%. Gadgil-Mukherjee (1991): population 60%, income distance 25%, fiscal performance 7.5%, special problems 7.5%.

Formulas

Harrod-Domar: g = s / ICOR. Savings 20% of GDP, ICOR 4: growth 5%.

Revision · Chapter 38Agriculture

Core idea

Agriculture is about 18.0% of GVA (2025-26) but about 43% of jobs (PLFS 2025). Policy rests on land, prices (MSP), food security (FCI, NFSA), inputs (fertiliser, PM-KISAN), markets and risk (PMFBY).

Definitions

  • MSP: announced before each sowing season on CACP recommendation, approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs; no statutory backing; 23 commodities (25 with toria and de-husked coconut, sugarcane via FRP).
  • Cost concepts: A2 = paid-out costs; A2+FL = A2 plus unpaid family labour; C2 = A2+FL plus rent and interest forgone on owned land and capital. Budget 2018-19: MSP at least 50% over A2+FL.
  • Economic cost; CIP: MSP plus procurement incidentals, storage, transport; Central Issue Price = price at which grain is issued to states. Consumer subsidy = economic cost − CIP.
  • FCI: 1965, Food Corporations Act 1964: price support, PDS supply, buffer stocks; buffer norm about 25 Mt of wheat and rice.
  • Land Acquisition Act 2013: consent: none for government use, 70% for PPP, 80% private; compensation 2 to 4 times market value.

Revision · Chapter 39Industry, MSMEs and Industrial Policy

Core idea

Manufacturing is 14.8% of GVA (2025-26) and 12.1% of jobs; it has stagnated near 15-16% of GDP since 1991. Policy: Make in India (2014), PLI schemes, MSME support, disinvestment, start-ups and Atmanirbhar Bharat.

Definitions

  • Make in India: September 2014; 27 sectors (15 manufacturing under DPIIT, 12 service under Commerce). Targets of 12-14% manufacturing growth, 25% of GDP and 100 million jobs were not met.
  • PLI: cash incentive of 4% to 6% on incremental sales over a base year, for five years; 14 sectors, outlay Rs 1.97 lakh crore. Example: sales Rs 1 lakh to 1.2 lakh at 4% = Rs 800.
  • MSME test: investment and turnover both within the limit; same for manufacturing and services; exports excluded from turnover (MSMED Act 2006; composite test July 2020).
  • Disinvestment: minority (token): government keeps 51% or more; strategic: sale of 50% or more with management transfer. DIPAM is the nodal department; Strategic Disinvestment Policy 2021.
  • Start-up (DPIIT): up to ten years old; turnover not above Rs 100 crore in any year; innovation or scalable model.
  • E-commerce FDI: 100% automatic in the marketplace model; none in the inventory model.
  • Atmanirbhar Bharat: 2020; five pillars: economy, infrastructure, system, demography, demand; no licensing, private sector welcomed.

Revision · Chapter 40Services and Digital

Core idea

Services are 54.3% of GVA (2025-26) but agriculture still holds about 43% of jobs: growth is services-led, employment is not. Digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, Account Aggregator, DigiLocker, ONDC, DBT) is the India Stack.

Definitions

  • DPI: shared, open, interoperable digital rails built by the state or public bodies on which private firms innovate.
  • India Stack layers: identity: Aadhaar (UIDAI); payments: UPI (NPCI); data: Account Aggregator (RBI-regulated, consent-based), DigiLocker; commerce: ONDC; DBT through JAM (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile).
  • GCC: Global Capability Centre: in-house centre of a multinational for engineering, analytics and operations; moves India from cost arbitrage to capability and R&D.
  • DPDP Act 2023: data protection law; rules notified November 2025, phased over 12-18 months; Data Protection Board adjudicates.

Revision · Chapter 41Poverty, Inequality and Human Development

Core idea

India's official poverty measure is consumption-based (Tendulkar 21.9%, Rangarajan 29.5% in 2011-12); no new official line exists. The NITI MPI shows 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23). Inequality is measured by the Gini coefficient; the demographic dividend peaks around 2041.

Definitions

  • Gini coefficient: area between the Lorenz curve and the line of equality ÷ area under the line of equality; 0 = equality, 1 = one person has everything.
  • Kuznets hypothesis: 1955: inequality first rises then falls with development (inverted U).
  • TFR: children per woman over child-bearing years; replacement about 2.1; India about 2.0.
  • Demographic dividend: growth from a rising working-age (20-59) to non-working-age ratio; peak about 2041, working-age about 59% (WA/NWA 1.43).
  • Unemployment rate: unemployed ÷ labour force × 100.
  • SECC 2011: automatically excluded (13 parameters), automatically included (5 destitution parameters), others (7 deprivation indicators); basis for PMAY-G, DAY-NRLM, Ayushman Bharat, Ujjwala.
  • National MPI: Alkire-Foster; 12 indicators in three equal dimensions: health, education, standard of living.

Formulas

Gini = A / (A + B), A = area between Lorenz curve and equality line. Unemployment rate = unemployed / (employed + unemployed) × 100.

Revision · Chapter 42Urbanisation and Demography

Core idea

Census 2011 counted 121.08 crore people; urbanisation rose from 27.81% (2001) to 31.16% (2011). SRS 2023 puts TFR at 1.9, below replacement 2.1. Census 2027 is India's first digital census and counts caste.

Definitions

  • Census town: administratively rural but population at least 5,000, at least 75% of male main workers non-agricultural, density at least 400 per sq. km.
  • Statutory town: governed by an urban local body.
  • Urban agglomeration: town with outgrowths or contiguous towns; includes a statutory town; population at least 20,000.
  • Million-plus; mega city: 10 lakh or more; 1 crore or more (Greater Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata).
  • Lee's push-pull model: 1966: origin (push), destination (pull), intervening obstacles, personal factors.
  • Harris-Todaro: 1970: migrate if expected urban wage exceeds rural wage; expected wage = W_u × (E_u / L_u). Todaro paradox: more urban jobs can raise urban unemployment.

Revision · Chapter 43Education and Health

Core idea

Elementary education is a fundamental right (Article 21A; RTE Act 2009, in force 1 April 2010); NEP 2020 sets 5+3+3+4 and 6% of GDP. Government health spending is 1.43% of GDP (NHA 2022-23); Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY gives Rs 5 lakh cover per family.

Definitions

  • NEP 2020: replaced NPE 1986; Kasturirangan committee; 5+3+3+4 (foundational, preparatory, middle, secondary); mother tongue till Grade 5, preferably 8; HECI as single regulator (excluding medical and legal); Academic Bank of Credit.
  • NEP targets: universal education ECCE to secondary and 100% GER by 2030; 50% higher-education GER by 2035; public spending 6% of GDP.
  • Data sources: UDISE+ (schools); AISHE (higher education); ASER (learning outcomes, Pratham).
  • National Health Policy 2017: public health spending to 2.5% of GDP by 2025; two-thirds to primary care; life expectancy 70; 2 beds per 1,000.
  • Ayushman Bharat: two arms: Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) and PM-JAY; funding 60:40 (Centre:states), 90:10 North-East and Himalayan states, 100% Centre for UTs without legislature.
  • ABDM: September 2021; National Health Authority; ABHA health ID, professional and facility registries.

Revision · Chapter 44Social Structure

Core idea

India follows principled distance in secularism (Articles 25-30), recognises 22 scheduled languages and 11 classical languages, and uses reservation (SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC 27%, EWS 10%) within a 50% cap that the EWS ruling (2022) treats as not immutable.

Definitions

  • Kymlicka: three group-differentiated rights: self-government, polyethnic, special representation; external protections yes, internal restrictions no.
  • Principled distance: Bhargava: state neither separates from religion nor identifies with one; sarva dharma sambhava.
  • Indra Sawhney (1992): upheld 27% OBC quota, set 50% cap and the creamy layer.
  • EWS: 103rd Amendment 2019 (Arts 15(6), 16(6)); family income below Rs 8 lakh; upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).
  • Melting pot vs salad bowl: assimilation (early US) vs cultural pluralism (Canada 1988, UK, India).
  • RPwD Act 2016: 21 disabilities; 4% of posts; at least 5% higher-education seats; free education 6 to 18.

Revision · Chapter 45Environment and Sustainable Development

Core idea

Sustainable development (Brundtland 1987) meets present needs without compromising future generations. The climate regime moved from binding Kyoto targets to voluntary Paris NDCs; India targets net zero by 2070 and 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 (300 GW crossed July 2026).

Definitions

  • CBDR: common but differentiated responsibilities (UNFCCC principle).
  • Panchamrit (COP-26, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil by 2030; 50% energy from renewables; cut 1 bn tonnes of emissions; 45% intensity cut; net zero 2070.
  • Carbon tools: carbon credit = permit for one tonne CO2e; cap and trade; carbon tax per tonne emitted.
  • Paris Agreement (COP-21, 2015): replaced Kyoto; well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; voluntary NDCs every five years; Article 6 carbon markets.
  • Constitutional basis: Article 48A (DPSP), Article 51A(g) (duty), Article 21 (clean environment).
  • EIA 2006: prior environmental clearance for listed projects; public consultation for most.

Revision · Chapter 46Farming Systems and the Food Economy

Core idea

Irrigation (tube wells, canals, wells, tanks), cropping patterns, livestock, GM and seed law, organic and natural farming, and the food-processing chain with its regulators (FSSAI, WDRA, ECA 1955).

Definitions

  • Cropping patterns: intercropping (rows); mixed (no fixed pattern); sequential (rice-wheat); relay (next crop sown before harvest); ratooning (regrowth from stubble).
  • GEAC: regulates GM crops under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986; Bt cotton (2002) is the only commercial GM crop; Bt brinjal moratorium since 2010.
  • PPVFR Act 2001: breeders get exclusive rights; farmers may save, sow, exchange, sell farm-saved seed (not branded); National Gene Fund.
  • NPOP vs PGS-India: NPOP: third-party, Commerce Ministry, APEDA secretariat, export and domestic; PGS-India: peer-based, Agriculture Ministry, domestic only. Sikkim first fully organic State (2016).
  • ZBNF: no purchased inputs (Bijamrit, Jivamrit, mulching, Waaphasa); contrasts with organic.
  • FSS Act 2006: replaced Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954; FSSAI under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, not the DGHS.
  • WDRA Act 2007: registers warehouses; negotiable warehouse receipts (electronic from 2017); e-NAM trading from April 2020.
  • Essential Commodities Act 1955: lets the Centre regulate supply and prices and impose stock limits.

Revision · Chapter 47Infrastructure

Core idea

Infrastructure is capital-intensive and long-gestation, so the public sector stays central; PPPs, VGF and monetisation bring in private capital. Union Budget 2026-27 capital expenditure is Rs 12.2 lakh crore.

Definitions

  • EPC: government pays a contractor to build and operates it; not a PPP.
  • PPP: private partner builds and operates under a concession through an SPV; risk to the party best able to bear it.
  • BOT; BOOT; DBFOT: build-operate-transfer; build-own-operate-transfer; design-build-finance-operate-transfer.
  • VGF: one-time upfront grant to make a viable but financially unviable PPP bankable.
  • Hybrid Annuity Model (2016): 40% of cost paid during construction, 60% as annuities after completion.
  • TOT: NHAI leases built highways (about 30 years) for an upfront payment.
  • InvIT / REIT: SEBI-regulated trusts; at least 80% in revenue-generating assets. NIIF (2015): 49% government stake.
  • Value capture finance: extra FAR premiums, land pooling, TDR, change-of-land-use fees.
